questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which of the following is considered an auxiliary flight control?
questions.explanation: Leading-edge flaps, speed brakes, spoilers, trailing-edge flaps, and leading-edge slats are auxiliary (secondary) wing flight control surfaces. Answer (A) is incorrect. A ruddervator is a primary, not auxiliary, flight control surface that incorporates both a rudder and an elevator into one surface. This is done on “V”-tail-type airplanes. Answer (B) is incorrect. Upper rudders (found on the B-727) are standby rudders, which are used in the event of a hydraulic system failure. These are primary, not auxiliary, flight controls.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which of the following is considered a primary flight control?
questions.explanation: The primary flight control surfaces allow the pilot to control an airplane’s movement around its lateral, longitudinal, and vertical axes. The primary flight controls are the elevator, ailerons, and rudder. Answer (A) is incorrect. Slats are high-lift devices, not a flight control device. Answer (C) is incorrect. A dorsal fin is not a flight control, but rather is used to provide directional stability.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which of the following are considered primary flight controls?
questions.explanation: The primary flight control surfaces allow the pilot to control an airplane’s movement around its lateral, longitudinal, and vertical axes. The primary flight controls are elevators, ailerons, and rudders. Answer (A) is incorrect. Tabs are secondary, not primary, flight controls. Answer (B) is incorrect. Flaps are secondary, not primary, flight controls.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When are inboard ailerons normally used?
questions.explanation: Some large aircraft use two sets of ailerons (inboard and outboard). At high airspeeds, the aerodynamic loads from use of the outboard ailerons twist the wingtips. The outboard ailerons are locked in the neutral position during high-speed flight. Answer (A) is incorrect. The inboard ailerons are used during both high-and low-speed flight. Answer (B) is incorrect. The inboard ailerons are used during both high-and low-speed flight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When are outboard ailerons normally used?
questions.explanation: Some large aircraft use two sets of ailerons (inboard and outboard). At high airspeeds, the aerodynamic loads from use of the outboard ailerons twist the wingtips. The outboard ailerons are locked in the neutral position during high-speed flight. Answer (B) is incorrect. The outboard ailerons are locked during high-speed flight. Answer (C) is incorrect. The outboard ailerons are locked during high-speed flight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Why do some airplanes equipped with inboard/ outboard ailerons use the outboards for slow flight only?

choices.text: Increased surface area provides greater controllability with flap extension.
Aerodynamic loads on the outboard ailerons tend to twist the wingtips at high speeds.
Locking out the outboard ailerons in high-speed flight provides variable flight control feel.

questions.explanation: Some large aircraft use two sets of ailerons (inboard and outboard). At high airspeeds, the aerodynamic loads from use of the outboard ailerons twist the wingtips. The outboard ailerons are locked in the neutral position during high-speed flight. Answer (A) is incorrect. While using the outboard ailerons during slow flight does increase roll stability, if they are used in high-speed flight, the aerodynamic loads would twist the wingtips. Answer (C) is incorrect. Locking out the outboard ailerons reduces the aerodynamic loads on the wings, preventing overstressing at high airspeeds.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the purpose of a control tab?

choices.text: Move the flight controls in the event of manual reversion.
Reduce control forces by deflecting in the proper direction to move a primary flight control.
Prevent a control surface from moving to a full-deflection position due to aerodynamic forces.

questions.explanation: When hydraulic pressure is lost to the primary controls, the control tabs unlock from their actuating cylinders and allow control wheel inputs. This method of secondary control is known as manual reversion. Answer (B) is incorrect. Servo, not control, tabs reduce control forces by deflecting primary flight controls in the proper direction. Answer (C) is incorrect. Anti-servo, not control, tabs prevent a control surface from moving to a full-deflection position due to aerodynamic forces.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the purpose of an elevator trim tab?

choices.text: Provide horizontal balance as airspeed is increased to allow hands-off flight.
Adjust the speed tail load for different airspeeds in flight allowing neutral control forces.
Modify the downward tail load for various airspeeds in flight eliminating flight-control pressures.

questions.explanation: The elevator trim tab acts on the elevators, which in turn act upon the entire airplane. This allows the pilot to adjust the angle of attack of the elevators, thus modifying the downward tail load for any airspeed in flight and eliminating the need to exert continuous flight-control pressures. Answer (A) is incorrect. The elevator trim tab permits hands-off flight at any airspeed, not only when the airspeed is increasing, and provides longitudinal, not horizontal, balance. Answer (B) is incorrect. The elevator trim tab adjusts the downward, not speed, tail load for various airspeeds in flight allowing neutral control forces.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which direction from the primary control surface does an elevator adjustable trim tab move when the control surface is moved?
questions.explanation: Once adjusted, an elevator adjustable trim tab remains fixed for all positions relative to the primary control surface as the primary control surface is moved. Answer (A) is incorrect. Adjustable trim tabs are adjusted in the opposite direction of the primary control surface as a means of trimming the control surface. Once adjusted, their relationship remains constant with respect to the primary control surface. Answer (B) is incorrect. Once adjusted, trim tabs remain fixed to the primary control surface as the primary control surface is moved.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the purpose of a servo tab?

choices.text: Move the flight controls in the event of manual reversion.
Reduce control forces by deflecting in the proper direction to move a primary flight control.
Prevent a control surface from moving to a full-deflection position due to aerodynamic forces.

questions.explanation: The servo tab aids the pilot in moving a primary control surface and in holding it in the desired position. Answer (A) is incorrect. In the event of manual reversion on some transport category aircraft, the control, not servo, tabs would move the flight controls. Answer (C) is incorrect. To preclude full deflection of control surfaces is the purpose of the anti-servo, not servo, tab.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which direction from the primary control surface does a servo tab move?
questions.explanation: Movement of the servo tab in one direction causes the primary control surface to move in the opposite direction. If a servo tab on an aileron is deflected upward, the aileron is deflected downward, increasing the angle of attack on that wing and resulting in greater lift on that wing. Answer (A) is incorrect. An anti-servo tab, as found on the trailing edge of stabilators, moves in the same direction as the stabilator to provide a feel to the pilot control pressures. Answer (C) is incorrect. Servo tabs move in response to the pilot’s control movements.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the purpose of an anti-servo tab?

choices.text: Move the flight controls in the event of manual reversion.
Reduce control forces by deflecting in the proper direction to move a primary flight control.
Prevent a control surface from moving to a full-deflection position due to aerodynamic forces.

questions.explanation: Since the anti-servo tab moves in the same direction as the control surface, it produces a stabilizing force that increases control force pressures. Answer (A) is incorrect. In the event of manual reversion, the control, not anti-servo, tabs would move the flight controls. Answer (B) is incorrect. A servo, not an anti-servo, tab reduces control forces by deflecting in the proper direction to move a primary flight control.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which direction from the primary control surface does an anti-servo tab move?
questions.explanation: An anti-servo tab, as found on the trailing edge of a stabilator, moves in the same direction as the primary flight control surface. Answer (B) is incorrect. A servo, not an anti-servo, tab moves in the opposite direction from the primary control surface. Answer (C) is incorrect. Trim, not anti-servo, tabs remain fixed during control inputs.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The primary purpose of high-lift devices is to increase the
questions.explanation: High-lift devices increase lift at low air-speeds, allowing lowered landing and takeoff speeds. Answer (A) is incorrect. Increasing the lift component is an objective of high-lift devices which increase the ratio of L/D. The primary purpose of high-lift devices is to increase lift at low speeds. Answer (C) is incorrect. Increasing the drag to reduce airspeed is the function of spoilers, not high-lift devices.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a purpose of leading-edge flaps?

choices.text: Increase the camber of the wing.
Direct airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack.

questions.explanation: The leading-edge flap is similar in operation to the plain flap. When actuated, the leading edge of the wing extends in a downward direction to increase the camber of the wing, providing greater lift at low flight speeds. Answer (B) is incorrect. Leading-edge flaps increase, not decrease, the lift at slow airspeeds. Answer (C) is incorrect. A slot, not a leading-edge flap, directs airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the primary function of the leading edge flaps in landing configuration during the flare before touchdown?
questions.explanation: The primary function of the leading edge flaps in the landing configuration during the flare before touchdown is to prevent flow separation at low airspeeds, therefore allowing lower landing and takeoff speeds. Answer (B) is incorrect. To decrease the rate of sink, the coefficient of lift (CL) must increase. CL is increased by the use of leading edge lift devices, slats, flaps, and other devices with the correct power setting. Answer (C) is incorrect. Spoilers, not leading edge flaps, increase profile drag and are usually deployed after touchdown to reduce lift.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect does the leading edge slot in the wing have on performance?

choices.text: Changes the stalling angle of attack to a higher angle.
Decelerates the upper surface boundary layer air.

questions.explanation: The leading edge slot in a wing conducts the flow of high energy air into the boundary layer on the upper surface and delays airflow separation to some higher angle of attack. Thus, the slot simply delays stall to a higher angle of attack. Answer (A) is incorrect. At low angles of attack, there is little or no profile drag increase. At high angles of attack, the slot delays the stall characteristics of the wing. Answer (C) is incorrect. The leading edge slot actually increases airflow on the upper wing surface to allow higher angles of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a purpose of leading-edge slats on high-performance wings?

choices.text: Increase lift at relative slow speeds.
Improve aileron control during low angles of attack.
Direct air from the low-pressure area under the leading edge along the top of the wing.

questions.explanation: Leading-edge slats direct air from the high-pressure area under the wing to the upper surface, resulting in improved stall characteristics at lower speeds. They also increase lift at relatively slow airspeeds. Answer (B) is incorrect. The leading edge slats are used during high, not low, angle of attack situations, such as takeoffs and landings. Answer (C) is incorrect. The area under the leading edge is high pressure, not low pressure.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a purpose of leading-edge slats on high-performance wings?

choices.text: Decrease lift at relative slow speeds.
Improve aileron control during low angles of attack.
Direct air from the high-pressure area under the leading edge along the top of the wing.

questions.explanation: Leading-edge slats direct air from the high-pressure area under the wing to the upper surface, resulting in improved stall characteristics at lower speeds. They also increase lift at relatively slow airspeeds. Answer (A) is incorrect. The purpose of leading-edge-lift slats is to increase, not decrease, the lift at low speeds. Sometimes these are referred to as high-lift devices. Answer (B) is incorrect. The leading-edge slats are used during high, not low, angle of attack situations, such as takeoffs and landings.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is a purpose of flight spoilers?

choices.text: Increase the camber of the wing.
Increase the rate of descent without increasing airspeed.
Direct airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack.

questions.explanation: Spoilers are mounted on the upper surface of each wing, and they reduce lift without increasing airspeed. Their purpose is to spoil or disrupt the smooth flow of air over the wing to reduce the lifting force of the wing, thus increasing the rate of descent without increasing airspeed. Answer (A) is incorrect. Flaps, not spoilers, increase the camber of the wing. Answer (C) is incorrect. Slots and slats, not spoilers, direct airflow over the top of the wing at high angles of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: For which purpose may flight spoilers be used?

choices.text: Reduce the wings’ lift upon landing.
Increase the rate of descent without increasing aerodynamic drag.
Aid in longitudinal balance when rolling an airplane into a turn.

questions.explanation: The purpose of spoilers is to spoil or disrupt the smooth flow of air over the wing to reduce the lifting force of the wing. Thus, flight spoilers may be used to reduce the wings’ lift upon landing. Answer (B) is incorrect. Spoilers will increase the aerodynamic drag. Answer (C) is incorrect. Longitudinal balance or stability is primarily achieved by the horizontal stabilizer, not a spoiler.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Flaps have more effect on
questions.explanation: The effectiveness of flaps on a wing configuration depends on many different factors. One important factor is the amount of the wing area affected by the flaps. The thicker the wing shape, the more effect the flaps have. Answer (B) is incorrect. Because surface area of the wing directly corresponds to flap effectiveness, thin wings are affected less, not more, than thicker wings. Answer (C) is incorrect. Symmetrical wings are generally less effective at producing lift due to their lack of positive upper camber. Because of this, flaps will result in less lifting force than if the wing shape were not symmetrical.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a purpose of ground spoilers?

choices.text: Reduce the wings’ lift upon landing.
Aid in rolling an airplane into a turn.
Increase the rate of descent without gaining airspeed.

questions.explanation: Spoilers are designed to spoil or disrupt the smooth flow of air over the wing to reduce the lifting force of the wing. Thus, ground spoilers are used to reduce the wings’ lift upon landing. Answer (B) is incorrect. A flight spoiler, not a ground spoiler, can be used to roll an airplane into a turn. Answer (C) is incorrect. Flight spoilers, not ground spoilers, are used to increase the rate of descent without gaining airspeed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Ground spoilers used after landing are
questions.explanation: Aerodynamic drag is initially the principal source of deceleration at high speed. As the speed lowers to 60-70% of landing speed, aerodynamic drag produced by ground spoilers is of little consequence. Answer (A) is incorrect. As the speed lowers to 60-70% of landing speed, aerodynamic drag produced by ground spoilers is of little consequence. Answer (B) is incorrect. Ground spoiler effectiveness is directly proportional to speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Split flaps as opposed to plain flaps

choices.text: produce more lift with less drag.
produce only slightly more lift, but much more drag.
enhance takeoff performance in hot temperatures and high altitudes.

questions.explanation: Split flaps produce slightly more lift than plain flaps, but they also produce more drag due to the turbulent airflow behind the wing. Answer (A) is incorrect. Although split flaps do produce slightly more lift than plain flaps, they produce more drag, not less. Answer (C) is incorrect. Both split flaps and plain flaps produce only slightly more lift when extended, but they create much greater drag. This combination of effects does not allow them to significantly enhance takeoff performance in high-temperature or high-altitude scenarios.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Fowler flaps as compared to split flaps

choices.text: generate more nose down pitching moment.
cause very little change in the airplane structure.

questions.explanation: The Fowler flap causes the greatest change in pitching moment, and the split flap causes the least. Answer (B) is incorrect. The split flap actually produces significantly more drag than the Fowler flap. Answer (C) is incorrect. Fowler flaps extend laterally, increasing the wing’s surface area. This movement significantly changes the airplane’s structure.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Fowler flaps as compared to split flaps

choices.text: generate more nose down pitching moment.
cause very little change in the airplane wing structure and characteristics.

questions.explanation: The Fowler flap causes the greatest change in pitching moment, and the split flap causes the least. Answer (B) is incorrect. The Fowler flap develops much more lift than the split flap. Answer (C) is incorrect. The Fowler flap design not only changes the camber of the wing, it also increases the wing area; this design significantly changes the airplane’s wing structure and characteristics.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Upon landing, spoilers

choices.text: decrease directional stability on the landing rollout.
function by increasing tire to ground friction.
should be extended after the thrust reversers have been deployed.

questions.explanation: When spoilers are deployed on landing, most of the wing’s lift is destroyed. This action transfers the airplane’s weight to the landing gear so that the wheel brakes are more effective. Answer (A) is incorrect. Spoilers increase, not decrease, directional stability on the landing rollout by transferring the airplane’s weight to the landing gear so the wheel brakes and nosewheel steering are more effective. Answer (C) is incorrect. Upon landing, spoilers should be extended immediately after touchdown, not after the thrust reversers have been deployed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: One method of boundary layer control is accomplished by injecting

choices.text: a jet of air into the leading edge to energize the boundary layer.
a low speed jet of air into the boundary layer.
a high speed jet of air into the boundary layer.

questions.explanation: Boundary layer control devices are an additional means of increasing the maximum lift coefficient of a section of the airfoil. Injecting a high-speed jet of air into the boundary layer when operating at high angles of attack can delay the onset of a stall. Answer (A) is incorrect. Injecting air into the leading edge does not aid in preventing boundary layer separation. In fact, this may increase boundary layer separation by decreasing the laminar flow of air across the upper wing surface. Answer (B) is incorrect. An injection of low-speed air into the boundary layer will not have any impact on preventing boundary layer separation.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: On most airplanes, the first 50% of flap deflection causes

choices.text: less than 50% of the total change in lift.
more than 50% of the total change in lift.
linear lift increases at the AFM specified speed.

questions.explanation: In most airplanes, the first 50% of flap deflection provides over half of the total lift capability of the flaps. The last 50% of flap deflection provides over half of the total drag increase of the flaps. Answer (A) is incorrect. In most airplanes, the first 50% of flap deflection provides over half, not less than half, of the total lift capability of the flaps. Answer (C) is incorrect. In most airplanes, the first 50% of flap deflection provides over half of the total lift capability of the flaps, not a linear lift increase.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Swept wings causes a significant
questions.explanation: Swept wings cause a reduction in effectiveness of flaps. Answer (A) is incorrect. Swept wings suffer from a reduction of flap effectiveness, not an increase in their effect. Answer (C) is incorrect. Flap actuation is not a reliability issue in swept wings, although the effectiveness of the flaps is reduced by the wing sweep.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Compared to a straight wing, swept wing flaps are
questions.explanation: The use of swept wings hinders the effectiveness of trailing edge control surfaces and high lift devices. Answer (A) is incorrect. The swept wing reduces the effectiveness of flaps. They are not equally effective to flaps installed on a straight wing. Answer (C) is incorrect. The swept wing reduces the effectiveness of flaps. They are not more effective than flaps installed on a straight wing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When at high angle of attack the boundary layer tends to

choices.text: loop around the upper camber line.
decrease air pressure along the chord.

questions.explanation: When at a high angle of attack, the boundary layer tends to stagnate and stop. The airflow will separate from the surface and a stall occurs. Answer (B) is incorrect. As the boundary layer stagnates, the airflow will separate and loop around the upper surface and a stall occurs. Answer (C) is incorrect. As the boundary layer separates from the body (curving above the upper camber of the wing) the pressure rises, resulting in a loss of lift as the critical angle of attack is reached.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: It is important to combine the boundary layer control with flaps since

choices.text: the flap deflection tends to reduce the angle of attack for maximum lift.
the flap deflection tends to increase the angle of attack for maximum lift.
the boundary layer controls are only effective at low power settings.

questions.explanation: Boundary layer control devices combined with flaps maintain high velocity smooth airflow with a maximum lift capability. Answer (B) is incorrect. The boundary layer control tends to increase the angle of attack, and the flaps help counter that increase by reducing, not increasing, the angle of attack for maximum lift. Answer (C) is incorrect. High speed air is required to maintain high velocity in the boundary layer to allay separation of the airflow.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the difference between the Fowler flap system and split flap system?

choices.text: Fowler flaps produce the greatest change in pitching moment.
Split flaps cause the greatest change in twisting loads.

questions.explanation: The types of flaps producing the greatest increases in aircraft lift coefficient, such as the Fowler flaps, produce the greatest twisting moment. The split flap causes more drag than lift and causes the least twisting moment. Answer (A) is incorrect. Fowler flaps produce a minimal amount of drag. Answer (C) is incorrect. Fowler flaps cause the greatest change in twisting moments while split flaps cause the least.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The tucking (downward motion) of the nose of an airplane during extension of Fowler flaps is

choices.text: a sign of contamination and a no flap landing may be necessary.

questions.explanation: A Fowler flap arrangement causes the greatest change in twisting moment. This causes the tucking of the nose. Answer (A) is incorrect. Aerodynamic twisting moments are normal and expected with a Fowler flap arrangement. Answer (C) is incorrect. Aerodynamic twisting moments are normal and are expected with the greatest change in moment from the Fowler flap.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Leading-edge, high-lift devices are

choices.text: more effective on the highly swept wing than trailing edge flaps.
less effective than a trailing edge device on a swept wing.
more effective than flaps because of the increase in drag at relatively low angles of attack.

questions.explanation: Leading-edge, high-lift devices are more effective on the highly swept wing than trailing edge flaps because they are more effective at creating additional lift. Trailing edge flaps normally cause more drag than lift, especially when fully deployed. Answer (B) is incorrect. Leading-edge, high-lift devices are more effective on a highly swept wing because they provide a powerful flow pattern. Answer (C) is incorrect. Slots will provide a negligible change in the pitching moment and no significant change in drag at low angles of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The first 50% of the flap deflection causes

choices.text: more than half of the total change in lift.
more than half of the total change in drag.

questions.explanation: The first 50% of flap deflection causes more than half the total change in the maximum coefficient of lift (CL ). Answer (B) is incorrect. The last 50% of flap deflection MAX causes more than half of the total change in drag, not the first 50% of flap deflection. Answer (C) is incorrect. The first 50% of flap deflection causes more than half the total change in lift.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What will be the ratio between airspeed and lift if the angle of attack and other factors remain constant and airspeed is doubled? Lift will be
questions.explanation: Lift is proportional to the square of the airplane’s velocity, if the angle of attack and other factors remain constant. For example, an airplane traveling at 200 kt. has four times the lift of the same airplane traveling at 100 kt. Answer (A) is incorrect. Lift is proportional to the square of the airplane’s velocity; it is not constant. Answer (B) is incorrect. As airspeed is doubled, the lift will be four times greater, not doubled.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What true airspeed and angle of attack should be used to generate the same amount of lift as altitude is increased?

choices.text: The same true airspeed and angle of attack.
A higher true airspeed for any given angle of attack.
A lower true airspeed and higher angle of attack.

questions.explanation: At an altitude of 18,000 ft., the air has one-half the density of air at sea level. Thus, in order to maintain the same amount of lift as altitude increases, an airplane must fly at a greater true airspeed for any given angle of attack. Answer (A) is incorrect. True airspeed must be increased, not constant, as altitude increases. Answer (C) is incorrect. True airspeed must increase, not decrease, for any given angle of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How can an airplane produce the same lift in ground effect as when out of ground effect?
questions.explanation: The reduction of the wingtip vortices due to ground effect alters the spanwise lift distribution and reduces the induced angle of attack and induced drag. The wing will require a lower angle of attack in ground effect to produce the same lift coefficient as when out of ground effect. Answer (A) is incorrect. If the same angle of attack is maintained, an increase in lift coefficient will result. Answer (C) is incorrect. A lower, not higher, angle of attack is required to produce the same lift in ground effect as out of ground effect.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: By changing the angle of attack of a wing, the pilot can control the airplane’s

choices.text: lift and airspeed, but not drag.

questions.explanation: Changes in the angle of attack can affect lift, airspeed, and drag. Answer (A) is incorrect. Gross weight cannot be controlled by angle of attack; however, the aircraft load factor may be altered with a change in angle of attack. Answer (B) is incorrect. Typically, at low angles of attack, the drag coefficient is low and small changes in angle of attack create only slight changes in the drag coefficient. At high angles of attack, small changes in the angle of attack cause significant changes in drag.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: In a jet powered airplane (fan or pure jet) the angle of attack at stall is

choices.text: very different from power on and power off.
essentially the same power on or power off.

questions.explanation: For a jet powered airplane (fan or pure jet), the angle of attack at stall is essentially the same whether power on or power off due to the lack of accelerated airflow moving over the wing surfaces. Answer (A) is incorrect. For a jet powered airplane (fan or pure jet), the angle of attack is essentially the same whether power on or power off, not variable with altitude. Answer (B) is incorrect. For a jet powered airplane (fan or pure jet), the angle of attack at stall is essentially the same whether power on or power off; it is not very different.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An increase in airspeed above the stall speed will require

choices.text: a relative decrease in the relative wind.
a corresponding decrease in angle of attack and co-efficient of lift.
a corresponding increase in co-efficient of lift and drag.

questions.explanation: An increase in airspeed above the stall speed requires a decrease of both angle of attack and the coefficient of lift. Answer (A) is incorrect. An increase in airspeed will result in an increase in relative wind, not a decrease. Answer (C) is incorrect. An increase in airspeed above stall speed will require a decrease in the coefficient of lift, not an increase. Although it is true, as this distractor answer suggests, that total drag will increase as speed increases.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Lift coefficient must be maximum at the
questions.explanation: The lift coefficient will be at its maximum value at the speed the airplane stalls. Answer (B) is incorrect. The airplane’s maximum maneuvering speed is based on a stall speed that occurs prior to an increase in load factor that would exceed the limit load for the aircraft. It is not predicated on maximum lift coefficient. Answer (C) is incorrect. VMMO is an operational limit speed, not a speed that corresponds to the maximum coefficient of lift, or the airplane’s stalling speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Propeller driven airplanes can develop more lift at slower airspeeds with high power on because

choices.text: the dynamic pressure is created downstream of the propellers.
the high power conditions decreases the maximum lift angle of attack.
the high power reduces the lift required from the wings.

questions.explanation: When the propeller driven airplane is at low airspeeds and high power, the dynamic pressure is much greater and causes considerably greater lift than at zero thrust. Answer (B) is incorrect. The high power conditions increase, not decrease, the maximum lift angle of attack. Answer (C) is incorrect. The wings still require the same amount of lift; however, the dynamic pressure provided from the propellers helps satisfy that requirement.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the effect on total drag of an aircraft if the airspeed decreases in level flight below that speed for maximum L/D?

choices.text: Drag increases because of increased induced drag.
Drag increases because of increased parasite drag.
Drag decreases because of lower induced drag.

questions.explanation: Total drag is at a minimum for the maximum lift-drag ratio (L/DMAX) at one specific angle of attack and lift coefficient. As airspeed decreases, the induced drag will increase because a greater angle of attack is required to maintain the lift coefficient. The amount of induced drag varies inversely as the square of the airspeed. Answer (B) is incorrect. Parasite drag varies directly, not inversely, with airspeed. Answer (C) is incorrect. Drag increases, not decreases, from any speed other than that for maximum L/D.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What performance is characteristic of flight at maximum L/D in a propeller-driven airplane?
questions.explanation: At maximum L/D, total drag is at a minimum. This occurs at a particular angle of attack and lift coefficient at which the proportion between speed and power required is the greatest. Thus, the maximum range and engine-out glide distance for a propeller-driven airplane is at maximum L/D. Answer (B) is incorrect. Best angle of climb (e.g., to clear an obstacle) is at a high angle of attack with both high lift and high drag coefficients, which would not result in a maximum L/D ratio. Answer (C) is incorrect. Maximum endurance would be obtained at the point of minimum power required, since this would require the lowest fuel flow to keep the airplane in steady, level flight. This point is not at maximum L/D.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What flight condition should be expected when an aircraft leaves ground effect?

choices.text: An increase in induced drag requiring a higher angle of attack.
A decrease in parasite drag permitting a lower angle of attack.

questions.explanation: The reduction of the wingtip vortices due to ground effect alters the spanwise lift distribution and reduces the induced angle of attack and induced drag. When leaving ground effect, the airplane will require an increase in angle of attack to maintain the same lift coefficient, which will increase induced drag. Answer (B) is incorrect. At slow airspeeds when taking off, induced, not parasite, drag predominates. Answer (C) is incorrect. When leaving ground effect, expect a decrease, not increase, in stability and a nose-up change in moment.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the relationship between induced and parasite drag when the gross weight is increased?

choices.text: Parasite drag increases more than induced drag.
Induced drag increases more than parasite drag.
Both parasite and induced drag are equally increased.

questions.explanation: Increasing airplane weight increases the induced drag (more lift is required) more than the parasite drag because a higher angle of attack is required to support the increased weight. Answer (A) is incorrect. Parasite drag increases less, not more, than induced drag as airplane weight increases. Answer (C) is incorrect. Induced drag increases more than parasite drag with increases in airplane gross weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: If the boundary layer separates

choices.text: the airflow separates from the wing surface and stall occurs.
ice will not sublime in this area.

questions.explanation: The boundary layer is the thick boundary that exists between the flow of air and the solid surface of the airfoil. If the boundary layer separates, the airflow separates as well, causing an increase in drag and a loss of lift that results in a stall. Answer (A) is incorrect. Drag increases with the separation of the boundary layer. It does not decrease due to the separation. Answer (C) is incorrect. The separation of the boundary layer affects airflow, lift, and drag in a relatively short duration manner. The result is an increase in drag and a stall. The sublimation of ice is not a factor in this situation.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An airplane flying at L/DMAX will have

choices.text: the same glide speed for all weights.
different glide ratios dependent on gross weight.
the same glide performance at all weights.

questions.explanation: Maximum glide performance (i.e., distance or range) is found at L/DMAX. Because this aerodynamic reference is determined at one specific angle of attack and lift coefficient, weight does not affect glide performance as long as the correct speed is maintained during the glide. Answer (A) is incorrect. An airplane’s glide speed increases with increases in weight. Answer (B) is incorrect. The maximum glide ratio for an airplane is found at L/DMAX. L/DMAX is a fixed aerodynamic point and does not vary based on weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Any angle of attack lower or higher than L/DMAX

choices.text: requires less thrust for steady state flight.
means less maneuvering margin before stalling.

questions.explanation: Any angle of attack lower or higher than that for L/DMAX increases the total drag for a given airplane. Answer (B) is incorrect. A lower or higher angle of attack will result in an increase in drag, which will require more thrust to maintain steady state flight, not less. Answer (C) is incorrect. An airplane can stall at any airspeed, in any attitude, based on exceeding the critical angle of attack, not a margin of maneuverability that exists between L/DMAX and a published stalling speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At the end of a power-on approach in a propeller driven airplane, if the pilot sharply reduces power,

choices.text: the airplane may continue to float for a long distance down the runway.
the airplane may drop suddenly due to reduced lift.
the airplane’s engine will quit running if the power is reduced suddenly.

questions.explanation: Airplanes with large propellers spinning rapidly in low pitch create considerable drag and may drop suddenly. In such airplanes, it is preferable to maintain power through the landing flare and touchdown. Answer (A) is incorrect. The airspeed will decay rapidly, not slowly, due to the increased drag caused by the propellers. Answer (C) is incorrect. The airplane should continue to run even if the power is reduced suddenly.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A bank angle of 15° will increase induced drag by about
questions.explanation: The equation used to determine this is: Load factor = Load factor = 2 Induced drag increase = 1.0353 = 1.072 To express as a percentage = (1.072 – 1) × 100 = 7.2% Answer (A) is incorrect. The increase of 3% would require a bank of about 5° at 1.015 Gs. Answer (C) is incorrect. The increase of 15% would require a bank of about 20° at 1.095 Gs.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A bank angle of 30° will increase induced drag by about
questions.explanation: A 33% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 30°. The equation used to determine this is: Load factor = Load factor = 2 Induced drag increase = 1.1547 = 1.3333 To express as a percentage = (1.3333 – 1) × 100 = 33.3% Answer (A) is incorrect. An 18% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 23°. Answer (C) is incorrect. A 24% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of about 28°.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A bank angle of 45° will increase induced drag by
questions.explanation: A 100% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 45°. The equation used to determine this is: Load factor = Load factor = 2 Induced drag increase = 1.4142 = 1.9999 To express as a percentage = (1.9999 – 1) × 100 = 99.9% Answer (A) is incorrect. A 33% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 30°. Answer (C) is incorrect. questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A bank angle of 60° will increase induced drag by
questions.explanation: A 300% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 60°. The equation used to determine this is: Load factor = Load factor = 2 Induced drag increase = 1.9999 = 3.9996 To express as a percentage = (3.9996 – 1) × 100 = 299.9% Answer (A) is incorrect. A 200% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 50°. Answer (C) is incorrect. A 100% increase in induced drag will be caused by a coordinated turn with a bank angle of 45°.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a purpose of wing-mounted vortex generators?

choices.text: Reduce the drag caused by supersonic flow over portions of the wing.
Increase the onset of drag divergence and aid in aileron effectiveness at high speed.
Break the airflow over the wing so the stall will progress from the root out to the tip of the wing.

questions.explanation: Rows of vortex generators located on the upper surface of the wing just upstream of the ailerons delay (reduce) the onset of drag divergence associated with supersonic airflow. Answer (B) is incorrect. Vortex generators decrease (delay) the onset of drag divergence, not increase the onset of drag divergence. Answer (C) is incorrect. A stall strip breaks the airflow over the wing so the stall will progress from the root out to the tip of the wing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What affects indicated stall speed?

choices.text: Load factor, angle of attack, and power.
Angle of attack, weight, and air density.

questions.explanation: An airplane’s indicated stall speed is affected by total airplane weight, weight distribution within the airplane, angle of bank, pitch attitude, control coordination, drag, and power settings, but NOT by angle of attack or air density. Answer (B) is incorrect. Indicated stall speed is not affected by the angle of attack. Answer (C) is incorrect. Indicated stall speed is not affected by angle of attack or air density.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a purpose of wing-mounted vortex generators?

choices.text: Delays the onset of drag divergence at high speeds and aids in maintaining aileron effectiveness at high speeds.
Breaks the airflow over the wing so the stall will progress from the root out to the tip of the wing.
Increase the onset of drag divergence and aid in aileron effectiveness at low speed.

questions.explanation: Rows of vortex generators located on the upper surface of the wing just upstream of the ailerons delay the onset of drag divergence at high speeds and also aid in maintaining aileron effectiveness at high speeds. Answer (B) is incorrect. Vortex generators do not break the airflow over the wing so the stall will progress from the root out to the tip of the wing. Answer (C) is incorrect. Vortex generators delay, not increase, the onset of drag divergence.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How can turbulent air cause an increase in stalling speed of an airfoil?

choices.text: An abrupt change in relative wind.
A decrease in angle of attack.

questions.explanation: Turbulence can cause an aircraft to stall at a significantly higher airspeed than in stable conditions. A vertical gust or wind shear can cause a sudden change in the relative wind and result in an abrupt increase in the angle of attack and, thus, result in a stall. Although a gust may not be maintained long enough for a stall to develop, the aircraft may stall while the pilot is attempting to control the flight path, particularly during an approach in gusty conditions. Answer (B) is incorrect. Decreased angle of attack decreases, not increases, the possibility of a stall. Answer (C) is incorrect. A sudden decrease in load factor decreases, not increases, the stalling speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Airflow separation over the wing can be delayed by using vortex generators,

choices.text: directing high pressure air over the top of the wing or flap through slots and making the wing surface smooth.
directing a suction over the top of the wing or flap through slots and making the wing surface smooth.
making the wing surface rough and/or directing high pressure air over the top of the wing or flap through slots.

questions.explanation: Airflow separation over the wing can be delayed by various methods of replacing the slow-moving laminar airflow next to the wing’s surface with faster-moving air. One method is the use of vortex generators, which are attached to the upper surface of the wing. Vortex generators make the wing surface rough, creating a turbulent flow that increases the speed of the air. Another method is to direct high-pressure air over the top of the wing or flap through slots. Answer (A) is incorrect. A smooth wing surface does not delay airflow separation. Vortex generators create a turbulent flow of air, which increases the speed of the airflow next to the wing’s surface. Answer (B) is incorrect. Vortex generators create a turbulent flow of air making the wing surface rough, not smooth. Additionally, slots direct high-pressure air, not a suction, over the top of the wing or flap.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An airplane stall warning device must sense
questions.explanation: The aircraft stalls when the critical angle of attack is exceeded. The angle of attack is measured as the angle between the chord line and the relative wind. In order to accurately warn of an impending stall, a stall warning device must sense the relative wind. Answer (B) is incorrect. Coincident wind is not a factor in determining that a stall is imminent. Answer (C) is incorrect. A stall warning device does not directly measure angle of attack. However, angle of attack indicators are frequently employed to avoid situations that would cause the stall warning system to initiate a warning.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How does VS (KTAS) speed vary with altitude?

choices.text: Remains the same at all altitudes.

questions.explanation: Due to the lesser pressure at altitude, a higher true airspeed is required to create the same pressure differential between impact (pitot) pressure and static air pressure. Consequently, true airspeed increases as altitude increases. Answer (A) is incorrect. True airspeed (TAS) increases with altitude; it does not remain unchanged. Answer (C) is incorrect. True airspeed varies directly with altitude, not inversely. As altitude increases, true airspeed increases.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Stall warning devices must sense
questions.explanation: Stall warning devices must sense pressure distribution on the wing in order to reliably indicate an impending stall. Answer (A) is incorrect. Static pressure is not a factor in determining when a stall is imminent. Answer (C) is incorrect. The measurement of dynamic pressures is important to the indication of airspeed, not stall warnings. This is primarily because the stall occurs as a result of exceeding an angle of attack at a specified pressure distribution. The combination that results in a stall can occur at any airspeed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An aircraft in a steady state, constant altitude turn

choices.text: experiences no changes in stall speeds.

questions.explanation: The stalling speed of an aircraft is higher in a level turn than in straight-and-level flight. This is due to the higher angle of attack required to maintain altitude, because a portion of vertical lift has been re-directed to horizontal lift. Answer (A) is incorrect. Airspeed indication errors result from a variety of factors, including excessive angle of attack, which is not typically experienced during a steady state, constant altitude turn. Answer (B) is incorrect. An airplane in a steady state, constant altitude turn will experience a stall at a higher airspeed than the same airplane in straight-and-level flight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An airplane will always stall at the same
questions.explanation: An aircraft stall results from a rapid decrease in lift caused by separation of airflow from the wing’s surface brought on by exceeding the critical angle of attack. A stall can occur at any pitch attitude or airspeed. The stalling speed of a particular aircraft is not a fixed value for all flight situations, but a given aircraft always stalls at the same angle of attack regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor, or density altitude. Answer (B) is incorrect. Regardless of the power setting or airspeed, a given aircraft will always stall at the same angle of attack. Answer (C) is incorrect. Regardless of the airspeed, a given aircraft will always stall at the same angle of attack.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Fundamental recovery from a stall requires
questions.explanation: To recover from a stall, you must decrease the angle of attack. While this action may involve lowering the pitch of the nose, increasing airspeed, and/or increasing power, decreasing the angle of attack is the fundamental way to recover from a stall. Answer (A) is incorrect. Increasing power alone will not cause the airplane to recover from a stall. Answer (B) is incorrect. Increasing airspeed alone will not cause the airplane to recover from a stall.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The stall speed of an airplane

choices.text: is constant regardless of weight or airfoil configuration.
is affected by weight and bank angle.
is not affected by dynamic pressures and lift coefficient.

questions.explanation: The stalling speed of an airplane is affected by both weight and bank angle. For example, the stalling speed of an aircraft is higher in a level turn than it is in straight-and-level flight. Answer (A) is incorrect. The stall speed of an airplane is not constant. Stall speed is affected by bank, weight, load factor, and power. Answer (C) is incorrect. Dynamic pressure and coefficient of lift are both considerations in wing design and performance. Their relationship does indeed have an effect on the stall speed of an airplane.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How does the stall speed (KCAS) vary as you climb from sea level to 33,000 feet?

choices.text: It varies directly with a change in altitude.
It remains relatively unchanged throughout the climb.
It varies indirectly with a change in altitude.

questions.explanation: Calibrated airspeed is derived from the airflow entering the pitot tube; the more air flowing through it, the greater the calibrated airspeed. As altitude increases, the density of the air decreases, and true airspeed increases. So, although the air is less dense, the increased true airspeed causes the same amount of air to enter the pitot tube as at lower altitudes, and the calibrated airspeed remains relatively unchanged throughout the climb. This air behaves the same way as it flows over the wings. Hence, the stall speed remains relatively unchanged throughout the climb even though true airspeed increases. Answer (A) is incorrect. True airspeed varies directly with a change in altitude; however, indicated and calibrated airspeed do not. Answer (C) is incorrect. Altitude has no effect on indicated or calibrated airspeed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A sudden pull-up after takeoff

choices.text: can result in a stall or spin.
will cause an increase in initial rate of climb.
will delay rotation, which may degrade acceleration.

questions.explanation: If the airplane is subject to a sudden pull-up or steep turn after becoming airborne, the result may be a stall, spin, or reduction in initial rate of climb. Answer (B) is incorrect. A sudden pull-up after takeoff may result in a reduction, not increase, in initial rate of climb. Answer (C) is incorrect. A delayed rotation is a typical takeoff error; however, when a sudden pull-up is initiated, the chances of a stall or spin are of concern.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is load factor?

choices.text: Lift multiplied by the total weight.
Lift subtracted from the total weight.
Lift divided by the total weight.

questions.explanation: A load factor is the ratio of the total airload acting on the airplane to the gross weight of the airplane. For example, if an airplane has a gross weight of 2,000 lb. and, during flight, is subjected to aerodynamic forces that increase the total load the wing must support to 4,000 lb., the load factor is 2 (4,000 ÷ 2,000). In this example, the airplane wing is producing lift that is equal to twice the gross weight of the airplane. Answer (A) is incorrect. Lift is divided, not multiplied, by the total weight. Answer (B) is incorrect. Lift is divided by, not subtracted from, the total weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: If an aircraft with a gross weight of 2,000 pounds were subjected to a total load of 6,000 pounds in flight, the load factor would be
questions.explanation: Load factor is the ratio of the total airload acting on the airplane to the gross weight of the airplane. In this problem, the total airload is 6,000 lb., and the gross weight is 2,000 lb. The load factor is 3 (6,000 ÷ 2,000). Load factors are usually expressed in terms of “G,” or pull of gravity, in this case, three times the actual weight. Answer (A) is incorrect. Calculating 6,000 lb. ÷ 2,000 lb. = 3, not 2. Answer (C) is incorrect. Calculating 6,000 lb. ÷ 2,000 lb. = 3, not 9.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Upon which factor does wing loading during a level coordinated turn in smooth air depend?
questions.explanation: The load factor for a given airplane during a level coordinated turn is determined solely by the angle of bank. Answer (A) is incorrect. In a coordinated turn, the rate of turn does not have any impact on the load factor, which is determined solely by the angle of bank. Answer (C) is incorrect. True airspeed has no impact on the load factor.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: For a given angle of bank, the load factor imposed on both the aircraft and pilot in a coordinated constant-altitude turn

choices.text: increases with an increase in airspeed.
remains constant regardless of airspeed changes.
decreases with an increase in airspeed.

questions.explanation: For any given angle of bank, the load factor of an airplane in a coordinated constant-altitude turn is dependent on the bank angle. It is not affected by airspeed changes. Answer (A) is incorrect. Increasing airspeed in a coordinated turn with a constant bank angle and altitude does not affect the load factor. Answer (C) is incorrect. Decreasing airspeed in a coordinated turn with a constant bank angle and altitude does not affect the load factor.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How does VNE change with altitude?

choices.text: remains the same at all altitudes.

questions.explanation: VNE remains the same. In an airplane, VNE is fixed and is marked on the airspeed indicator. It is not altered by altitude. Answer (B) is incorrect. VNE varies inversely with altitude in helicopters, not airplanes. Answer (C) is incorrect. The radial red line on the airspeed indicator is the value of VNE. That value will not change with altitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What result does a level turn have on the total lift required and load factor with a constant airspeed?

choices.text: Lift required remains constant, and the load factor increases.
Both total lift required and load factor increase.
Lift required increases, and the load factor decreases.

questions.explanation: In a constant airspeed, level turn both the total lift required and the load factor increase. Answer (A) is incorrect. The amount of lift required increases in a level turn at constant airspeed. It does not remain constant. Answer (C) is incorrect. The load factor increases in a constant airspeed, level turn. It does not decrease.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: While executing a 60° level turn, your aircraft is at a load factor of 2.0. What does this mean?

choices.text: The total load on the aircraft’s structure is two times its weight.
The load factor is over the load limit.
The gust factor is two times the total load limit.

questions.explanation: A load factor of 2.0 means the total load on an aircraft’s structure is two times its weight. Since load factors are expressed in terms of Gs, a load factor of 2.0 may be spoken of as 2 Gs and a load factor of 4.0 as 4 Gs. Answer (B) is incorrect. A load factor of 2.0 would be within all category load factor limits. The maximum safe load factors (limit load factors) are as follows: normal category airplanes are limited to 3.8 and –1.52 Gs, utility aircraft are limited to 4.4 and –1.76 Gs, and aerobatic aircraft are limited to 6.0 and –3.0 Gs. Answer (C) is incorrect. The gust factor is an increasing function of speed. A load factor of 2.0 does not reference a gust factor but rather the total load on an aircraft’s structure, which would be two times its weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At which speed will increasing the pitch attitude cause an airplane to climb?
questions.explanation: At speeds below L/DMAX, an increase in pitch will slow the airplane down (i.e., the region of reverse command). At L/DMAX and above, an increase in pitch will increase climb or decrease descent. Answer (A) is incorrect. Below L/DMAX, performance decreases, not increases, with increases in pitch. Answer (C) is incorrect. Below L/DMAX, performance decreases, not increases, with increases in pitch.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At what speed, with reference to L/DMAX, does maximum rate-of-climb for a jet airplane occur?

choices.text: A speed greater than that for L/DMAX.
A speed equal to that for L/DMAX.
A speed less than that for L/DMAX.

questions.explanation: The maximum rate-of-climb for a jet airplane will occur at a speed greater than that for L/DMAX. This occurrence is accounted for, in part, by the increase in power available with speed. Answer (B) is incorrect. A speed equal to that of L/DMAX is the maximum climb angle, not rate-of-climb. Answer (C) is incorrect. The maximum rate-of-climb is at a speed greater, not less, than L/DMAX.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect does an increase in airspeed have on a coordinated turn while maintaining a constant angle of bank and altitude?

choices.text: The rate of turn will decrease resulting in a decreased load factor.
The rate of turn will increase resulting in an increased load factor.
The rate of turn will decrease resulting in no changes in load factor.

questions.explanation: Increasing airspeed while maintaining a coordinated turn with a constant angle of bank and altitude will decrease the rate of turn. For any given bank angle, the rate of turn varies with the airspeed; the higher the speed, the slower the rate of turn. This variation compensates for added centrifugal force, allowing the load factor to remain the same. Answer (A) is incorrect. At a constant bank angle, the higher airspeed will decrease the rate of turn to compensate for added centrifugal force, allowing the load factor to remain the same, not decrease. Answer (B) is incorrect. For any bank angle, the rate of turn varies with the airspeed; the higher the speed, the slower, not faster, the rate of turn.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: During a skidding turn to the right, what is the relationship between the component of lift and centrifugal force?

choices.text: Centrifugal force is less than the horizontal lift component, and the load factor is increased.
Centrifugal force is greater than the horizontal lift component.
Centrifugal force and the horizontal lift component are equal, and the load factor is decreased.

questions.explanation: When centrifugal force is greater than the horizontal component of lift, the aircraft skids to the outside of the turn. Answer (A) is incorrect. Centrifugal force is greater than the horizontal lift component in a skidding turn. It is a slipping turn that results from centrifugal force being less than the horizontal component of lift. Answer (C) is incorrect. Centrifugal force and the horizontal component would be equal only in a coordinated turn. In a skidding turn, the centrifugal force must be greater than the horizontal component of lift.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: If no corrective action is taken by the pilot as angle of bank is increased, how is the vertical component of lift and sink rate affected?

choices.text: Lift increases and the sink rate increases.
Lift decreases and the sink rate decreases.
Lift decreases and the sink rate increases.

questions.explanation: As the angle of bank is increased, the horizontal component of lift increases, which decreases the vertical component. As this happens, weight is greater than the vertical component of lift, and lift decreases as the sink rate increases. Answer (A) is incorrect. Lift will decrease, not increase. Answer (B) is incorrect. The sink rate increases, not decreases, as the lift decreases.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the relationship of the rate of turn with the radius of turn with a constant angle of bank but increasing airspeed?

choices.text: Rate will decrease and radius will increase.
Rate will increase and radius will decrease.

questions.explanation: As airspeed is increased, the angle of attack needs to be decreased, which will cause the rate of turn to decrease. At the same time, the increase in airspeed results in an increase of the turn radius. Answer (B) is incorrect. To maintain a constant angle of bank while increasing airspeed, the radius of turn will increase, not decrease. Answer (C) is incorrect. To maintain a constant angle of bank while increasing airspeed, the rate of turn will decrease, not increase.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When turning, how can the pilot increase the rate of turn while decreasing the turn radius?

choices.text: Steepen the bank and increase airspeed.
Steepen the bank and decrease airspeed.
Shallow the bank and increase airspeed.

questions.explanation: At slower airspeeds, an airplane can make a turn in less distance (smaller radius) and at a faster rate. Thus, to decrease the radius and increase the rate of turn, one steepens the bank and decreases airspeed. Answer (A) is incorrect. A decrease, not increase, in airspeed decreases the turn radius. Answer (C) is incorrect. A shallow bank will decrease the rate of turn, and an increase in airspeed will increase the turn radius.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Why must the angle of attack be increased during a turn to maintain altitude?

choices.text: Compensate for loss of vertical component of lift.
Increase the horizontal component of lift equal to the vertical component.

questions.explanation: The lift during a turn is divided into two components, one vertical and the other horizontal. This division reduces the amount of lift that is opposing gravity. The angle of attack must be increased until the vertical component of lift is equal to the weight in order to maintain altitude. Answer (B) is incorrect. Angle of attack is increased in order to increase the vertical component of lift to equal weight. Answer (C) is incorrect. Additional thrust (power), not angle of attack, is used to compensate for increase in drag.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Generally, the turning performance of an airplane is defined by

choices.text: structural and power limits at high altitude.
aerodynamic and structural limits at low altitude.
control and structural limits at high altitude.

questions.explanation: Each of the three limiting factors (aerodynamic, structural, and power) may combine to define the turning performance of an airplane. Generally, aerodynamic and structural limits predominate at low altitude while aerodynamic and power limits predominate at high altitude. Answer (A) is incorrect. Aerodynamic, structural, and power limitations may combine to define the turning performance of an airplane. Generally, structural limitations are limited to lower altitudes due to the thinner air at higher altitudes. At higher altitudes, aerodynamic and power limitations generally apply. Answer (C) is incorrect. Aerodynamic, structural, and power limitations may combine to define the turning performance of an airplane. Generally, structural and aerodynamic limits predominate at lower altitudes due to thicker air. Control is not one of the recognized limiting factors of turning performance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An increase in airspeed followed by a decrease in control effectiveness may result in

choices.text: a decrease in downwash on the horizontal tail, resulting in a “tuck under.”
an increase in downwash on the horizontal tail, resulting in a “tuck under.”
the need for retrimming due to the increased speed.

questions.explanation: When airflow separation occurs on the wing due to shock wave formation resulting from an increase in speed, there will be a loss of lift and subsequent loss of downwash aft of the affected area. If there is a decrease in downwash on the horizontal tail, it will create a diving moment and the aircraft will “tuck under.” Answer (B) is incorrect. A decrease in downwash, rather than an increase in downwash, may cause a “tuck under.” Answer (C) is incorrect. There will not necessarily be a need for retrimming, rather the decrease in control effectiveness resulting by a large increase in airspeed may cause a “tuck under.”

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Describe dynamic longitudinal stability.
questions.explanation: Longitudinal stability is the quality that makes an airplane stable about its lateral axis. It involves the pitching motion as the airplane’s nose moves up and down in flight. Dynamic stability is the overall tendency that the airplane displays after its equilibrium is disturbed. Answer (A) is incorrect. Motion about the airplane’s longitudinal axis is lateral, not longitudinal, stability. Answer (C) is incorrect. Motion about the vertical axis is directional, not longitudinal, stability.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is a characteristic of longitudinal instability?

choices.text: Aircraft constantly tries to pitch down.

questions.explanation: Longitudinal stability is the quality that makes an airplane stable about its lateral axis (pitching). A longitudinally unstable airplane has a tendency to dive or climb (oscillations) progressively into a very steep dive or climb. Answer (B) is incorrect. Longitudinal stability refers to pitch, not bank, oscillations. Answer (C) is incorrect. The aircraft constantly trying to pitch down is a characteristic of improper elevator trim, not longitudinal instability.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Identify the type stability if the aircraft attitude remains in the new position after the controls have been neutralized.
questions.explanation: If the airplane’s nose remains in the new position after the elevator control is pressed forward and released, the aircraft displays neutral longitudinal static stability. Answer (A) is incorrect. A negative longitudinal static stability means the airplane tends to move even farther from the original position. Answer (B) is incorrect. With neutral longitudinal dynamic stability, the airplane continues to oscillate without a tendency to increase or decrease.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Identify the type stability if the aircraft attitude tends to move farther from its original position after the controls have been neutralized.
questions.explanation: When the airplane’s nose moves farther from its original position, it has the undesirable characteristic of negative static stability. Answer (B) is incorrect. Negative dynamic stability refers to oscillations that become progressively larger. Answer (C) is incorrect. If the aircraft had positive static stability, it would return to its original position.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Identify the type stability if the aircraft attitude tends to return to its original position after the controls have been neutralized.
questions.explanation: Imagine that you trim the airplane for hands-off control in level flight and then momentarily give the controls a slight push to nose the airplane down. If within a brief period the nose rises to the original position and then stops, the airplane is statically stable. It is positively statically stable because it has returned to its original position after being displaced. Answer (A) is incorrect. Positive dynamic stability refers to oscillations being dampened or decreasing. Answer (C) is incorrect. Neutral dynamic stability refers to oscillations continuing without a tendency to increase or decrease.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The engine thrustline

choices.text: has very limited influence on flight stability.
has no effect on stability in turbojets or fanjets.

questions.explanation: The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability. If the thrustline is below the center of gravity (CG), thrust produces a positive or nose-up moment and the effect is destabilizing. If the thrust line is located above the CG, a negative moment is created and the effect is stabilizing. Answer (A) is incorrect. Engine thrustline can cause an aircraft to be stable or unstable. Answer (B) is incorrect. The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability and is more noticeable in turbojets or fanjets.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Some airplanes can experience compressibility effects at flight speeds well below the speed of sound due to

choices.text: improperly compensated and adjusted trim surfaces.
surfaces that produce different local flow velocities.

questions.explanation: Every aircraft has a distinct aerodynamic shape that develops lift differently. Local flow velocities over some surfaces will be greater than the flight speed because of the way this airflow is handled. Answer (A) is incorrect. All components of the aircraft are affected by compressibility in some manner, and the effect of the interference between the various surfaces of the aircraft must be considered. However, it is the aerodynamic shape of the surfaces, not the improper adjustments, that typically cause the compressibility effects at speeds below that of sound. Answer (B) is incorrect. Compressibility effects relate to the air pressure and density changes that take place at high speeds, not the structural pressures on the airframe in the event of turbulence.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The engine’s thrust line above the center of gravity

choices.text: has little effect on the stability of the aircraft.

questions.explanation: If the thrust line is located above the center of gravity, a negative moment is created and the effect is stabilizing. Answer (A) is incorrect. If the thrust line is located above the CG, a negative moment is created and the effect is stabilizing. Answer (C) is incorrect. If the thrust line is located above the CG, a negative moment is created and the effect is stabilizing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The engine’s thrust line below the center of gravity

choices.text: has little effect on the stability of the aircraft.

questions.explanation: If the thrust line is below the center of gravity, thrust produces a positive, or nose-up, moment and the effect is destabilizing. Answer (B) is incorrect. The engine’s thrust line below the CG produces a positive, or nose-up, moment, which does not stabilize the aircraft. Answer (C) is incorrect. The engine’s thrust line below the CG produces a positive, or nose-up, moment, which does have an effect on the stability of the aircraft. The vertical location of the thrust line defines one of the direct contributions to stability.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What are some characteristics of an airplane loaded with the CG at the aft limit?

choices.text: Lowest stall speed, lowest cruise speed, and highest stability.
Highest stall speed, highest cruise speed, and least stability.
Lowest stall speed, highest cruise speed, and least stability.

questions.explanation: The airplane will stall at a higher speed with a forward CG location. The critical angle of attack is reached at a higher speed due to increased wing loading. Conversely, the airplane will stall at a lower speed with an aft CG loading. The airplane will cruise faster with an aft CG location because of reduced drag. The airplane will become less stable as the CG is moved rearward. Answer (A) is incorrect. An aft CG causes an airplane to have the highest, not lowest, cruise speed and the least, not highest, stability. Answer (B) is incorrect. An aft CG causes the airplane to have the lowest, not highest, stall speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What characteristic should exist if an airplane is loaded to the rear of its CG range?
questions.explanation: The rearward CG limit is largely determined by considerations of stability. When loaded to the rear of its CG limit, an airplane will become unstable about the lateral axis, i.e., longitudinally unstable. At this point when the nose is momentarily pulled up, it may alternately climb and dive, becoming steeper with each oscillation. Answer (A) is incorrect. An aft location of the CG has a greater effect on the longitudinal stability, not the lateral (aileron) controllability. Answer (B) is incorrect. An aft CG has a greater effect on the longitudinal stability, not vertical (rudder) controllability.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An airplane loaded with the Center of Gravity (CG) aft of the rear CG limit could

choices.text: make it easier to recover from stalls and spins.
make it more difficult to flare for landing.
increase the likelihood of inadvertent overstress.

questions.explanation: The increased instability from an aft CG makes the aircraft more difficult to flare for landing. Answer (A) is incorrect. As the CG of the aircraft moves aft, the aircraft becomes progressively more unstable, making the recovery from a stall or spin more difficult. Answer (C) is incorrect. The major factor in overstressing is excess weight either exceeding the overall weight limit of the aircraft or exceeding the weight limit for a certain area, such as a baggage compartment.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An airplane loaded with the CG at the aft limit will

choices.text: be very unbalanced in lateral control forces.
feel heavy in the longitudinal axis.

questions.explanation: An airplane loaded with the CG at the aft limit will fly more efficiently. The drag is reduced because a smaller angle of attack and less downward deflection are required of the horizontal stabilizer. Answer (B) is incorrect. Having an aft CG does not effect the balance of the airplane along its lateral axis. The airplane will fly more efficiently with an aft CG because of the need for less downforce on the horizontal stabilizer and the corresponding decrease in drag. Answer (C) is incorrect. An aft CG allows the airplane to fly more efficiently with less downforce required from the horizontal stabilizer. An aft CG can also create a heavy feel in the longitudinal axis, but this is less exaggerated as long as the CG remains within the aircraft’s limits.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At the aft CG limit the horizontal stab and elevator

choices.text: must develop less down force to balance the decreased forward loading.
will require less movement to maintain level flight.
can be trimmed to closer to neutral and be very heavy on the controls.

questions.explanation: The elevator or stabilator normally produce the down force required to hold the nose up against the nose-down pitching moment of the wing. As the CG moves aft, the amount of down force needed to counter the nose-down pitching moment decreases, therefore the elevator or stabilator does not need to develop as much down force. Answer (B) is incorrect. The further aft CG becomes, the less down force is needed to maintain level flight. This will require less movement and more less pressure on the controls to maintain level flight. Answer (C) is incorrect. The trim would have to be set for a lower nose-up attitude with aft CG however this would not make the controls very heavy.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
