questions.question: (Refer to Figure 229 on page 231 and Figure 231 on page 232.) Given the following conditions, what is the takeoff climb limit? Airport OAT: 38°C Airport Pressure Altitude: 14 ft. Flaps: 15° Engine Bleed for packs: On Anti-ice: Off
questions.explanation: First find 38°C on the horizontal axis, by estimating 8/10ths of the distance between 30°C and 40°C. Next go straight up to the 0 ft. pressure altitude line (this is the best estimate for 14 ft.) and, at this point, go straight across to the climb limit brake release weight of 136,000 pounds. Answer (B) is incorrect. The climb limit brake release weight is 136,000 pounds. Answer (C) is incorrect. The climb limit brake release weight is 136,000 pounds.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 229 on page 231.) Given the following conditions, what is the takeoff field limit weight? Temperature (OAT): 30°C Pressure Altitude: 5,431 ft. Field length available: 12,000 ft. Runway slope, Up: 1% Wind (KTS) Headwind: 20 Engine Bleed for Packs: On Anti-ice: Off
questions.explanation: On the Takeoff Field Limit Chart, first find 12,000 ft. on the horizontal axis for field length available. Go up to the first reference line, then follow the runway slope line to 1% up. Then go straight up to the next reference line and follow the wind line up to 20 kts. headwind. From this point, draw a line straight up the rest of the chart. Now find 30°C on the horizontal axis for the Airport OAT, and go straight up to the pressure altitude lines and stop halfway between the 5,000 ft. and 6,000 ft. pressure altitude lines. Next go horizontally across to the limit weight reference line, then follow the direction of limit weight lines until you intersect with the line you previously drew straight up the chart, from the headwind lines. From the intersection of these two lines, go horizontally across to find the field length limit brake release weight of 160,000 pounds. Answer (B) is incorrect. The field length limit brake release weight is 160,000 pounds. Answer (C) is incorrect. The field length limit brake release weight is 160,000 pounds.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect does an uphill runway slope have upon takeoff performance?
questions.explanation: The upslope of a runway impedes acceleration, resulting in a longer ground run on takeoff. Answer (B) is incorrect. Indicated airspeed for takeoff remains the same. Answer (C) is incorrect. The takeoff distance is increased, not decreased.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect does landing at high elevation airports have on groundspeed with comparable conditions relative to temperature, wind, and airplane weight?

choices.text: The same as at low elevation.

questions.explanation: An airplane at altitude will land at the same indicated airspeed as at sea level but, because of the reduced density (comparable conditions), the true airspeed (TAS) will be greater. Thus, with a higher TAS, the ground speed will be higher at high elevation airports than at low elevation. Answer (B) is incorrect. At high elevation, there is reduced air density, and thus TAS will increase. As TAS increases, groundspeed will increase, not decrease. Answer (C) is incorrect. Under comparable conditions, TAS will increase and cause the groundspeed to be higher, not the same, at higher elevation.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which condition reduces the required runway for takeoff?
questions.explanation: The effect of a headwind is to allow the airplane to reach lift-off speed at a lower groundspeed. A headwind that is 10% of the takeoff airspeed will reduce the takeoff distance approximately 19%. Answer (A) is incorrect. Higher-than-recommended airspeed before rotation increases, not reduces, the required runway for takeoff. Answer (B) is incorrect. Lower-than-standard air density increases, not decreases, the required runway for takeoff.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which performance factor decreases as airplane gross weight increases, for a given runway?
questions.explanation: Critical engine failure speed (i.e., takeoff decision speed, or V1) is the speed to which the airplane can be accelerated, lose an engine, and then either continue the takeoff with the remaining engine(s) or stop, in the same total runway distance. Critical engine failure speed decreases as the airplane gross weight increases due to the increased mass that must decelerate and stop in the event of a rejected takeoff. Answer (B) is incorrect. An increase in aircraft gross weight usually results in an increase in the rotation speed (VR). Answer (C) is incorrect. The accelerate-stop distance will increase as the aircraft gross weight increases.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Under which condition during the landing roll are the main wheel brakes at maximum effectiveness?

choices.text: When wing lift has been reduced.
When the wheels are locked and skidding.

questions.explanation: During the landing roll, the main wheel brakes are at maximum effectiveness when wing lift has been reduced and the normal force on the wheels approaches the weight of the airplane. At this point, the braking friction force is at maximum. Answer (B) is incorrect. At high groundspeeds, the lift is greater and the normal force on the wheels is small; thus, the braking friction force is small. Answer (C) is incorrect. When the wheels are locked and skidding, the braking friction force is small.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Arriving over the runway threshold 100 ft. high (150 HAT) would add approximately how many feet to the landing distance?
questions.explanation: A common approach error is excessive height over the threshold. This could be the result of an unstable approach or a stable but high approach. It also may occur during an instrument approach where the missed approach point is close to or at the runway threshold. Excessive height over the threshold will most likely result in a touchdown beyond the normal aiming point. An extra 50 feet of height over the threshold will add approximately 1,000 feet to the landing distance. It is essential that the airplane arrive at the approach threshold window exactly on altitude (50 feet above the runway). Answer (A) is incorrect. Arriving over the runway threshold 50 feet high would cause an added 1,000 feet of landing distance. Answer (B) is incorrect. Arriving over the runway threshold 75 feet high would cause an added 1,500 feet of landing distance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Approaching the runway 1° below glidepath can add how many feet to the landing distance?
questions.explanation: If the pilot crosses the threshold at an angle shallower than the normal 3°, the shallow approach angle effectively increases the landing distance and should be avoided. An approach angle of 2° instead of a recommended 3° will add 500 feet to landing distance. Answer (A) is incorrect. Approaching the runway 0.5° below glidepath, not 1° below glidepath, can add approximately 250 feet to the landing distance. Answer (C) is incorrect. Approaching the runway 2° below glidepath, not 1° below glidepath, can add approximately 1,000 feet to the landing distance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Arriving over the runway 10 knots over VREF would add approximately how many feet to the dry landing distance?
questions.explanation: Ten knots of excess airspeed will delay touchdown by approximately 2,500 feet due to floating in the flare and add approximately 300 feet to the ground roll after touchdown on a dry runway. Thus, the total amount added to the dry landing distance would be approximately 2,800 feet. Answer (A) is incorrect. Arriving over the runway 3 knots over VREF, not 10 knots, would add approximately 800 feet to the dry landing distance. Answer (B) is incorrect. Arriving over the runway 6 knots over VREF, not 10 knots, would add approximately 1,700 feet to the dry landing distance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 232 on page 235.) Given the following conditions, what is the takeoff climb limit? Airport OAT: 30°C Airport Pressure Altitude: 5431 ft. Flaps: 25° Engine Bleed for packs: On Anti-ice: Off
questions.explanation: Find 30°C on the horizontal axis. Go straight up and estimate 5,431 ft., halfway between the 5,000 ft. and 6,000 ft. pressure altitude lines. Now go straight across to the climb limit brake release weight of 116,000 pounds. Answer (B) is incorrect. The climb limit brake release weight is 116,000 pounds. Answer (C) is incorrect. The climb limit brake release weight is 116,000 pounds.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: One typical takeoff error is

choices.text: delayed rotation which may extend the climb distance.
premature rotation which may increase takeoff distance.
extended rotation which may degrade acceleration.

questions.explanation: Premature rotation may increase takeoff distance. If the aircraft does not have sufficient airspeed to fly, it may settle back onto the runway. Answer (A) is incorrect. Delayed rotation will result in a higher takeoff speed, not an extended climb distance. Answer (C) is incorrect. An extended rotation does not degrade acceleration, although over-rotation can create additional drag that can degrade acceleration. Establishing an appropriate attitude for VX or VY will allow the aircraft to safely leave ground effect and accelerate normally.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: During takeoff

choices.text: pitch control is a relatively minor skill requirement.
pitch rotation is not an important factor in performance calculations for distance and obstacle clearances.
insufficient pitch rotation may result in increased rolling resistance and excessive landing gear speeds.

questions.explanation: Insufficient rotation may provide added rolling resistance or require that the airplane accelerate to some excessive speed prior to becoming airborne. Answer (A) is incorrect. Any item which alters the takeoff velocity or acceleration during takeoff roll will affect the takeoff distance. Having the proper skillset to rotate appropriately is an important skill requirement. Answer (B) is incorrect. Pitch rotation is an important factor and technique for takeoff performance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A landing weight increase of 10% will result in a landing distance increase of approximately
questions.explanation: A 10% increase in landing weight will result in an increase in landing distance by 10%. Answer (A) is incorrect. An increase of 7% landing distance would result from a landing weight increase of about 7%, not 10%. Answer (C) is incorrect. An increase of 15% landing distance would result from a landing weight increase of about 15%, not 10%.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 230 on page 237.) Given the following conditions, what is the takeoff field limit weight? Temperature (OAT): 38°C Pressure Altitude: 14 ft. Field length available: 9,401 ft. Runway slope: 0% Wind (KTS) Tailwind: 3 Engine bleed for packs: On Anti-ice: Off
questions.explanation: On the Takeoff Field Limit – Dry Runway chart, first find 9,400 ft. on the horizontal axis for Field Length Available. Go straight up to the first reference line and, as there is no runway slope, continue straight up to the second reference line for wind correction. Follow the tailwind line back to 3 kts. (approximately 1/4 of the distance from 0 to –10 kts. tailwind). Now draw a line straight up the chart. Next find 38°C on the horizontal axis for Airport OAT by estimating 8/10ths of the distance between 30°C and 40°C. From here, go straight up to the 0 ft. pressure altitude line (this is the best estimate for 14 ft.). Then go horizontally across to the limit weight reference line and follow the direction of limit weight lines until you intersect with the line you previously drew straight up the chart from the tailwind lines. From the intersection of these two lines, go horizontally across to find the field length limit brake release weight of 169,000 pounds. Answer (A) is incorrect. The field length limit brake release weight is 169,000 lb. Answer (C) is incorrect. The field length limit brake release weight is 169,000 lb.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: You touchdown long with a speed of 145 knots on a 9,001-foot runway and the braking is not working, so you decide to takeoff and climbout. The engines require 5 seconds to spool up and then the airplane requires 10 seconds of acceleration to liftoff again. The 5,000-foot runway distance remaining sign flashes by. Do you have enough runway to liftoff? (Use 142 knots for average groundspeed due to the tailwind.)

choices.text: Yes, there will be a margin of about 850 feet with almost 3 seconds of decision time.
Yes, there will be a margin of almost 1,401 feet which allows about 5.8 seconds of decision time.
No, the runway is 1,104 feet too short and my decision is about 3 seconds too late.

questions.explanation: Given that 1 NM = 6,076.1 feet, use the following formula to determine the distance covered during the 15 seconds required for the engines to spool up to takeoff thrust and for the airplane to accelerate to V2: [(142 × 6,076.1) ÷ 3,600] × 15 = 3,595 feet Since 5,000 ft. of runway remains, you have a margin of about 1,405 ft. of runway length. At the speed you are moving down the runway, you will have a little less than 6 seconds of time to make and implement this decision. Answer (A) is incorrect. This answer would require approximately 17 seconds of delay instead of 15 seconds. Answer (C) is incorrect. This answer would require an average speed of 242 kt. instead of 142 kt.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Excessive takeoff speeds may result in approximately a

choices.text: 4% takeoff distance increase for each 1% of additional takeoff speed.
1% takeoff distance increase for each 2% of additional takeoff speed.
2% takeoff distance increase for each 1% of additional takeoff speed.

questions.explanation: Takeoff distance varies with the square of takeoff velocity if one assumes acceleration is constant. Rudimentary physics uses the following equation to determine the relationship between velocity, acceleration, and distance for uniformly accelerated objects. S = Acceleration distance in feet V = Velocity in feet per second, after uniformly accelerating from a velocity of zero a = Acceleration in feet per second Assume the aircraft has a takeoff velocity of 150 kt. (253.5 feet per second) with an acceleration of .2 g (6.434 feet per second). A 1% increase in takeoff velocity is computed by multiplying the takeoff velocity by 0.01. 253.5 × .01 = 2.53 253.5 + 2.53 = 256.03 Now compute the new takeoff distance. Takeoff distance increased by 100 feet (2%). 100 ÷ 4,994 = .02 Answer (A) is incorrect. A 4% increase in takeoff speed would result in a 4% increase in takeoff distance. Answer (B) is incorrect. A 1% increase in takeoff speed would result in a 2% increase in takeoff distance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: You are rolling out after touchdown and decide you really need to abort your landing, and takeoff. Your airplane is at 116 knots and your engines have spooled down to 71% idle. You need a V2 of 142 to safely lift off and climb. The airplane will require 6 seconds to accelerate after the engines spool up to takeoff thrust, which requires 4 seconds. How much runway will you require for a safe landing abort from your decision point? (Use an average of 129 knots ground speed.)
questions.explanation: Given that 1 NM = 6,076.1 feet, use the following formula to determine the distance covered during the 10 seconds required for the engines to spool up to takeoff thrust and for the airplane to accelerate to V2: Answer (A) is incorrect. A runway length of 1,738 feet would be required if 8 seconds, not 10 seconds, were required for the engines to spool up to takeoff thrust and for the airplane to accelerate to V2. Answer (C) is incorrect. A runway length of 3,601 feet would be required if 16.5 seconds, not 10 seconds, were required for the engines to spool up to takeoff thrust and for the airplane to accelerate to V2.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A landing weight increase of 10% will result in
questions.explanation: A 10% increase in landing weight will produce a 21% increase in the kinetic energy of the airplane that must be dissipated during the landing roll. Answer (A) is incorrect. A 3% increase in landing weight will produce about a 7% increase in the kinetic energy of the airplane that must be dissipated during the landing roll. Answer (C) is incorrect. A 16% increase in landing weight will produce a 33% increase in the kinetic energy of the airplane that must be dissipated during the landing roll.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Aerodynamic braking becomes ineffective

choices.text: at speeds less than 60% to 70% of touchdown speed.
at speeds greater than 60% to 70% of touchdown speed.

questions.explanation: At speeds less than 60% to 70% of the touchdown speed, aerodynamic drag is so slight that it is of little use and braking must be utilized to produce continued deceleration. Answer (B) is incorrect. Aerodynamic braking becomes ineffective at speeds less than 60% to 70% of the touchdown speed, not at speeds greater than 60% to 70% of touchdown speed. Answer (C) is incorrect. Aerodynamic braking becomes ineffective at speeds less than 60% to 70% of the touchdown speed, not any time after touchdown.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Aerodynamic braking is only effective to approximately
questions.explanation: The use of aerodynamic drag is applicable only for deceleration to 60% to 70% of the touchdown speed. At speeds less than 60% to 70% of the touchdown speed, aerodynamic drag (braking) is so slight that it is of little use and braking must be utilized for continued deceleration. Answer (A) is incorrect. At 30% of the touchdown speeds, aerodynamic drag has little consequence to braking. Answer (B) is incorrect. At 40% to 50% of the touchdown speed, aerodynamic drag has little consequence to braking.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: For airplanes with relatively low thrust-to-weight ratios, a 10% increase in takeoff gross weight would result in a takeoff distance increase of approximately
questions.explanation: For the airplane that has a 10% takeoff gross weight, with a relatively low thrust-to-weight ratio, the result in the increase in takeoff distance would be approximately 25% to 30%. Answer (A) is incorrect. For the airplane with a 5% takeoff gross weight, with a relatively low thrust-to-weight ratio, the result in the increase in takeoff distance would be approximately 14%. Answer (B) is incorrect. For the airplane with an 8% takeoff gross weight, with a relatively low thrust-to-weight ratio, the result in the increase in takeoff distance would be approximately 23%.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 233 on page 241.) Given the following conditions, what is the obstacle climb limit? Obstacle height: 522 ft. Distance from brake release: 9000 ft. OAT: 38°C Pressure Altitude: 427 ft. Wind (Kts.) Headwind: 8 kts. Flaps: 15° Engine Bleed for packs: On Anti-ice: Off
questions.explanation: On the Obstacle Limit chart, first estimate 522 ft. on the horizontal axis for obstacle height, using 500 feet. Go straight across to 9,000 ft. for distance from brake release, halfway between the 8,000 ft. and 10,000 ft. curves. From this point, go straight up to the reference line for OAT and follow the temperature line up to 38°C by estimating 8/10ths of the distance from 30°C to 40°C. Now go straight up to the pressure altitude reference line and follow the pressure altitude line to approximately 427 ft., halfway between 0 ft. and 1,000 feet. From here, go straight up to the wind reference line and follow the headwind line up to 8 kts., just before the 10 kt. line. Go straight up to the obstacle limit weight of 92,500 pounds. Answer (B) is incorrect. The obstacle limit weight is 92,500 pounds. Answer (C) is incorrect. The obstacle limit weight is 92,500 pounds.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 239 above.) Given the following conditions, what is the takeoff %N1? OAT (°F): 85° Airport Pressure Altitude (FT): 5431 ft. Engine bleeds for packs: Off Anti-ice: Off
questions.explanation: On the Takeoff %N1 chart, find figures for 80°F and 90°F and interpolate for 85°F, for each of 5,000 ft. and 6,000 ft. pressure altitude, to find 95.95 and 95.85. Now interpolate for 5,500 ft. to find 95.9. Go to the %N1 Adjustments for Engine Bleeds Chart below and find 0.8 for 5,500 ft. Add this to the takeoff %N1: 95.9 0.8 = 96.7%. Answer (A) is incorrect. This percentage would result if you subtracted instead of added 0.8% to 95.9%. Answer (B) is incorrect. This percentage would result if you did not add the adjustment for engine bleeds.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 234 on page 243.) Given the following conditions, what is the brake energy limits VMBE? Airport Pressure Altitude: 5431 ft. Brake Release Weight: 160,000 lbs. Airport OAT: –18°C Runway Slope (Up): 1% Wind (Kts.) Headwind: 10 kts.
questions.explanation: On the Brake Energy Limits VMBE chart, estimate 5,431 ft. on the vertical axis for pressure altitude by using 5,400 ft. on the seventh increment between 4,000 ft. and 6,000 ft. Go straight across to the –18°C line for Airport OAT. From here, go straight down to the 160,000 lbs. line for Brake Release Weight. Now go straight across to 162 kts. for VMBE. Now adjust VMBE for 1% up slope by adding 2 kts., giving 164 kts., and adjust this for 10 kts. headwind by adding 4 kts., giving a final VMBE of 168 knots. Answer (A) is incorrect. The brake energy limits VMBE is 168 kts. Answer (B) is incorrect. The brake energy limits VMBE is 168 kts.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A headwind that is 10% of the landing speed will decrease the landing distance
questions.explanation: A headwind which is 10% of the landing airspeed will reduce the landing distance 19%. Answer (A) is incorrect. A headwind which is 5% of the landing airspeed will reduce the landing distance by approximately 11%. Answer (C) is incorrect. A headwind which is 15% of the landing airspeed will reduce the landing distance by approximately 24%.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 41 on page 245.) Given the following, what is the single-engine climb or descent performance? Pressure altitude 3,000 ft Temperature (OAT) +35 °C
questions.explanation: Find a pressure altitude of 3,000 ft on the left side of the chart. Move horizontally to the right until you meet the point in the middle of the arcs for +30° and +40° OAT. Now move vertically down to find a rate of –100 ft/min, indicating a descent. Answer (A) is incorrect. A descent rate of 175 ft/min would be the approximate answer at +40° OAT. Answer (C) is incorrect. A climb rate of 350 ft/min would be the approximate answer at –40° OAT.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 237 on page 247 and Figure 238 on page 248.) Given the following conditions, what are the takeoff V speeds? Weight: 170,000 lb. Flaps: 15° Temperature (OAT): 16°C Field pressure altitude: 5431 ft. Runway slope: 1% Wind (KTS) Headwind: 10 KTS Runway condition: Dry Runway For VR: More than or equal to .1 VR = round up VR (ex: 140.1 = 141)

choices.text: V1 139 kts., VR 137 kts., V2 141 kts.
V1 138 kts., VR 138 kts., V2 141 kts.
V1 137 kts., VR 137 kts., V2 140 kts.

questions.explanation: Go to Fig. 237 (Takeoff Speeds – Dry Runway), enter the Takeoff Speeds table at 170,000 lb. and go across to Flaps 15 to find V1 136, VR 136, and V2 141. Find the adjustments in the second table by entering the table at 16°C and interpolating for 5,500 ft. pressure altitude. Rounding up for any VR or above, gives V1 139, VR 138, and V2 141. Adjusting V1 for runway slope and wind gives V1 140; however, V1 cannot exceed VR, so V1 is 138, VR is 138, and V2 is 141. Answer (A) is incorrect. These speeds would result if you did not adjust V1 to be equal to VR (i.e., it cannot be higher), and VR is not rounded up after interpolating for 5,500 ft. pressure altitude. Answer (C) is incorrect. These speeds would result if you only adjusted V1 for runway slope and wind. VR and V2 are not rounded up after interpolating for 5,500 ft. pressure altitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 237 on page 247 and Figure 238 on page 248.) Given the following conditions, what are the takeoff V speeds? Weight: 170,000 lb. Flaps: 10° Temperature (OAT): 25°C Field pressure altitude: 427 ft. Runway slope: 0% Wind (KTS) headwind: 8 KTS Runway condition: Wet Runway For VR more than or equal to .1 VR, round up VR to the next value (example: 140 + .1 = 141)

choices.text: V1 134 kts., VR 140 kts., V2 145 kts.
V1 140 kts., VR 140 kts., V2 145 kts.
V1 138 kts., VR 141 kts., V2 145 kts.

questions.explanation: Go to Fig. 238 (Takeoff Speeds – Wet Runway), enter the Takeoff Speeds Chart at 170,000 lb. and, under Flaps 10, find V1 133 kts., VR 139 kts., and V2 145 knots. Enter the adjustments table at 27°C and interpolate for 500 feet. Round down to 133 kts. for V1, up to 140 kts. for VR (must always round up if .1 or above) and no adjustment for V2 145 knots. No adjustments are necessary for runway slope, but one knot should be added for wind effects. The final speeds are V1 134 kts., VR 140 kts., and V2 145 knots. Answer (B) is incorrect. Speeds for VR and V2 are correct; however, V1 is 134 kts., not 140 knots. Answer (C) is incorrect. V1 is 134 kts., not 138 kts., and VR is 140 kts., not 141 knots.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 240 above.) Given the following conditions, what is the stab trim setting? Weight: 160,000 lb. CG (%MAC): 24% Flaps: 15°
questions.explanation: On the Stab Trim Setting chart, go to the second table for Flaps 10, 15, and 25. Find the weight row of 160-180 (1,000 lb.) and go across to 24% MAC, where you will come to 5 1/2%. Answer (A) is incorrect. This percentage would result if you used the table for Flaps 1 and 5, not Flaps 15. Answer (C) is incorrect. This percentage would result if you used 30% MAC, not 24% MAC.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which maximum range factor decreases as weight decreases?
questions.explanation: For propeller-driven airplanes, maximum range is obtained at maximum lift-drag (L/D) ratio, the point at which the proportion between speed and power required is greatest. As weight decreases, so does this optimum airspeed due to a reduction in the maximum L/D. Additionally, for jet aircraft, airspeed must be reduced as weight decreases to obtain maximum range. Answer (A) is incorrect. The factors of maximum range are weight, altitude, and aerodynamic configuration of the airplane, not angle of attack. Answer (B) is incorrect. Maximum range altitude may increase, not decrease, with a decrease in weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What should a pilot do to maintain “best range” airplane performance when a tailwind is encountered?
questions.explanation: A pilot flying an airplane in a tailwind should decrease speed to take advantage of the wind. In a headwind, the pilot should increase speed to reduce the effect of the wind. Answer (A) is incorrect. A pilot would increase speed with a headwind, not a tailwind. Answer (B) is incorrect. A pilot would maintain speed in a calm wind, not tailwind, condition.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which procedure produces the minimum fuel consumption for a given leg of the cruise flight?

choices.text: Increase altitude for a headwind, decrease altitude for a tailwind.

questions.explanation: Airplanes flying in a headwind should fly at higher airspeeds to reduce the effect of the headwind. Conversely, airplanes flying in a tailwind should slow to take advantage of the wind with lower power settings. Answer (B) is incorrect. Tailwind increases performance, and slower TAS decreases fuel consumption. Answer (C) is incorrect. Airspeed, not altitude, should be adjusted according to the wind.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At what speed, with reference to L/DMAX, does maximum range for a jet airplane occur?

choices.text: A speed less than that for L/DMAX.
A speed equal to that for L/DMAX.
A speed greater than that for L/DMAX.

questions.explanation: Maximum range for a jet airplane occurs when the proportion between velocity and thrust required is greatest, and this point is at a speed greater than that for L/DMAX. Answer (A) is incorrect. A speed greater, not less, than L/DMAX will obtain maximum range for a jet airplane. Answer (B) is incorrect. A speed equal to that of L/DMAX is a jet airplane’s maximum endurance, not maximum range.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Maximum range performance of a turbojet aircraft is obtained by which procedure as aircraft weight reduces?
questions.explanation: Maximum range is the consideration of maximum flying distance. “Cruise control” of an airplane implies that the airplane is operated to maintain the recommended long-range cruise condition throughout the flight. As fuel is consumed, the gross weight will vary and optimum airspeed, altitude, and power setting can vary. As the gross weight decreases, the optimum airspeed and power may decrease, or the optimum altitude may increase. Answer (A) is incorrect. As weight decreases, the optimum speed decreases, not increases, or altitude increases. Answer (C) is incorrect. As weight decreases, speed decreases, not increases, or altitude increases, not decreases.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The increase in specific range with altitude of the turbojet airplane can be attributed to three factors. One of those factors is

choices.text: an increase in altitude in the troposphere results in higher energy air flow.
an increase in proportion of velocity verses thrust required.

questions.explanation: An increase in altitude will increase the proportion of V/Tr and provide a greater TAS for the same Tr. Answer (A) is incorrect. An increase in altitude in the troposphere will produce lower inlet air temperature and air flow. Answer (C) is incorrect. An increase in altitude increases the engine RPM speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The most important factor affecting the specific range of a turbojet airplane is

choices.text: the decrease of the proportion of V/Tr (where V = velocity and Tr = thrust required).

questions.explanation: The effect of altitude on the range of the turbojet airplane is of great importance because no other single factor can cause such large variations of a specific range. Answer (B) is incorrect. A decrease in RPM is the result of altitude, not a factor affecting the range. There will be a decrease in engine RPM at altitude, but it will require an increase in engine RPM or the same amount of thrust. Answer (C) is incorrect. There will actually be an increase in the proportion of V/Tr and a greater TAS for the same Tr.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The specific fuel consumption of a turbojet climbing above the tropopause

choices.text: will continue to decrease as altitude increases.
will remain constant as altitude increases.

questions.explanation: Altitudes much above the tropopause bring about a general deterioration of overall engine efficiency and the specific fuel consumption begins to increase with altitude. Answer (A) is incorrect. Above the tropopause, the temperature is constant and altitudes slightly above the tropopause cause no further decrease in fuel consumption. In fact, fuel consumption will begin to increase with altitude. Answer (B) is incorrect. Generally, the specific fuel consumption decreases steadily with altitude until the tropopause is reached. Fuel consumption tends to increase above the tropopause.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The most efficient cruise control in a turbojet is
questions.explanation: The climbing cruise takes advantage of the benefits of optimum altitudes during cruise and results in a more efficient flight path. Answer (B) is incorrect. A flight idle descent is very efficient; however, it would not provide a usable cruise. Answer (C) is incorrect. A constant altitude cruise requires a reduction of airspeed and engine thrust to maintain optimum lift. It does not take advantage of the higher altitudes rendering it less efficient than the climbing cruise.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The specific range for a turbojet at 40,000 feet is approximately

choices.text: 150% greater than obtained at sea level.
150% greater than obtained at ground level.
125% greater than obtained at sea level.

questions.explanation: The typical turbojet airplane obtains a specific range at 40,000 feet, which is approximately 150% greater than that obtained at sea level. Answer (B) is incorrect. This performance is measured above sea level, not above ground level. Answer (C) is incorrect. At 40,000 feet, the turbojet will have a 150%, not 125%, higher specific range than at sea level.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At 3,000 feet with a temperature of 95°F and a calibrated airspeed of 100 knots, your true airspeed is
questions.explanation: Using an E6B flight computer, convert 95°F to 35°C from the temperature conversion scale. Line up 3,000 feet pressure altitude with 35°C in the pressure altitude window. Find calibrated airspeed of 100 on the outer scale of the inner wheel. This will be indicated as the number 10. Read the true airspeed above 10. It should be lined up almost with 109. The closest answer is 10 knots higher than the calibrated airspeed of 100 knots. Answer (A) is incorrect. A true airspeed of 15 knots higher would require a calibrated airspeed of 105 knots. Answer (C) is incorrect. A true airspeed of 5 knots higher would require a calibrated airspeed of 96 knots.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the reason for variations in geometric pitch along a propeller or rotor blade?

choices.text: It permits a relatively constant angle of attack along its length when in cruising flight.
It prevents the portion of the blade near the hub or root from stalling during cruising flight.
It permits a relatively constant angle of incidence along its length when in cruising flight.

questions.explanation: Variations in the geometric pitch of the blades permit the propeller to operate with a relatively constant angle of attack along its length when in cruising flight. Propeller blades have variations to change the blade in proportion to the differences in speed of rotation along the length of the propeller and thereby keep thrust more nearly equalized along this length. Answer (B) is incorrect. If there were no variation in geometric pitch, the propeller tips, not the root, would be stalled during cruising flight. Answer (C) is incorrect. Variations in geometric pitch permit a constant angle of attack, not incidence, along its length.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect does high relative humidity have upon the maximum power output of modern aircraft engines?

choices.text: Neither turbojet nor reciprocating engines are affected.
Reciprocating engines will experience a significant loss of BHP.
Turbojet engines will experience a significant loss of thrust.

questions.explanation: Water vapor, i.e., high relative humidity, will cause a significant reduction of power output of reciprocating engines but a negligible loss of thrust for a turbojet engine. Answer (A) is incorrect. Both reciprocating and turbojet engines are affected by high relative humidity. Answer (C) is incorrect. Turbojet engines will have a negligible, not significant, loss of thrust.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Under normal operating conditions, which combination of MAP and RPM produce the most severe wear, fatigue, and damage to high performance reciprocating engines?
questions.explanation: The most severe rate of wear and fatigue damage occurs at high RPM and low MAP on engines found on transport category airplanes, such as a DC-6. High RPM produces high centrifugal loads and reciprocating inertia loads. Thus, operating time at maximum RPM and MAP must be held to a minimum, and operation at maximum RPM and low MAP must be avoided. See page 145 of Aerodynamics for Naval Aviators. Note that this is the opposite from what we learn as commercial pilots regarding current high-performance engines. Answer (B) is incorrect. High, not low, RPM and low, not high, MAP produce the most severe wear to high-performance reciprocating engines. Answer (C) is incorrect. A high RPM and a low, not high, MAP produce the most severe wear to high-performance reciprocating engines.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Where is the critical altitude of a supercharged-reciprocating engine?

choices.text: The highest altitude at which a desired manifold pressure can be obtained.
Highest altitude where the mixture can be leaned to best power ratio.
The altitude at which maximum allowable BMEP can be obtained.

questions.explanation: Because the density of air decreases as altitude increases, the supercharger compresses the thin air to maintain the preset power (manifold pressure) as the airplane climbs. When the critical altitude is reached, the turbine is rotating at its highest speed and can no longer compensate for decreasing manifold pressure after that altitude is exceeded. Answer (B) is incorrect. Critical altitude is the highest altitude at which a manifold pressure, not fuel mixture, can be obtained. Answer (C) is incorrect. BMEP is pressure representing the mean gas load on the piston during the power stroke, not the air pressure in the manifold.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is controlled by the waste gate of a turbocharged-reciprocating engine?
questions.explanation: The waste gate allows exhaust gas to be directed to drive the turbine of the turbocharger. The waste gate is normally controlled automatically to maintain the required amount of exhaust gas flow so the turbocharger can maintain the desired manifold pressure. At the critical altitude, the exhaust gas waste gate is fully closed, and the turbine is operating at maximum speed. Answer (A) is incorrect. The waste gate controls exhaust gas discharge, not a supercharger gear ratio. Answer (C) is incorrect. The throttle opening sets the desired manifold pressure; it does not operate a waste gate that is part of the turbocharger system.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Under what condition should stalls never be practiced in a twin-engine airplane?

choices.text: With full flaps and gear extended.

questions.explanation: The pilot of a twin-engine airplane should become familiar with imminent stalls entered with various flap settings, power settings, and landing gear positions. Because of possible loss of control, stalls with one engine inoperative or at idle power and the other developing effective power are not to be practiced. Answer (B) is incorrect. You may be required to practice stalls with climb power on. Answer (C) is incorrect. Stalls should be practiced with full flaps and gear extended, as in a stall on approach to landing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What does the blue radial line on the airspeed indicator of a light, twin-engine airplane represent?

choices.text: Minimum controllable airspeed for single-engine operation.

questions.explanation: The airspeed indicator of a light, twin-engine airplane is marked (in addition to other normally marked airspeeds) with a red radial line at the minimum controllable airspeed with the critical engine inoperative, and a blue radial line at the best rate-of-climb airspeed with one engine inoperative. Answer (B) is incorrect. The blue radial line is the maximum single-engine rate, not angle, of climb. Answer (C) is incorrect. Minimum controllable airspeed for single-engine operation is marked by a red, not blue, radial line.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What performance should a pilot of a light, twin-engine airplane be able to maintain at VMC?

choices.text: Heading, altitude, and ability to climb 50 ft./min.

questions.explanation: VMC represents the minimum controllable airspeed with a critical engine inoperative. FAA regulations require that, in an airplane at VMC, the pilot must at least be able to stop the turn that results when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative within 20° of the original heading using max rudder deflection and a max bank of 5° into the operative engine. Also, after recovery, the pilot must maintain the airplane in straight flight with not more than 5° bank wing lowered toward the operating engine. This does not mean that the airplane must be able to climb or even to hold altitude. It means only that a heading can be maintained. Answer (B) is incorrect. The ability to maintain altitude is not a requirement of VMC. Answer (C) is incorrect. The ability to hold altitude and climb is not a requirement of VMC.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect, if any, does altitude have on VMC for an airplane with unsupercharged engines?
questions.explanation: For an airplane with unsupercharged engines, VMC decreases as altitude is increased; i.e., directional control can be maintained at a lower airspeed than at sea level. VMC is a function of power, which decreases with altitude. It is possible for the airplane to reach a stall speed prior to the loss of directional control. Answer (A) is incorrect. VMC is always affected by altitude. Answer (B) is incorrect. VMC decreases, not increases, with altitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Under what condition is VMC the highest?

choices.text: Gross weight is at the maximum allowable value.
CG is at the most rearward allowable position.
CG is at the most forward allowable position.

questions.explanation: VMC is greater when the center of gravity is at the most rearward allowable position. Since the airplane rotates around its center of gravity, the moments are measured using that point as a reference. A rearward CG would not affect the thrust moment but would shorten the arm to the center of the rudder’s horizontal lift, which would mean that a higher force or airspeed would be required to provide the necessary rudder effectiveness. Answer (A) is incorrect. Maximum gross weight decreases, not increases, VMC. Answer (C) is incorrect. A forward CG increases rudder effectiveness and reduces VMC.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the resulting performance loss when one engine on a twin-engine airplane fails?

choices.text: Reduction of cruise airspeed by 50 percent.
Reduction of climb performance of 80-90 percent or more.
Reduction of all performance by 50 percent.

questions.explanation: When one engine fails on a light twin, the most obvious problem is the loss of 50% of power. When power is increased in both engines in level flight and airspeed is held constant, the airplane will climb at a rate depending on the power added. When one engine fails, however, not only does it lose power, but the drag increases considerably because of asymmetric thrust. The operating engine must carry the full burden alone, and climb performance may be reduced by 80-90% or more. Answer (A) is incorrect. The power loss affects climb capability much more than it does cruise speed. Answer (C) is incorrect. Power is reduced by 50%, and climb performance is reduced by 80-90% or more.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which engine is the “critical” engine of a twin-engine airplane?

choices.text: The one with the center of thrust closest to the centerline of the fuselage.
The one designated by the manufacturer because it develops most usable thrust.
The one with the center of thrust farthest from the centerline of the fuselage.

questions.explanation: On twin-engine airplanes, if the propellers rotate in the same direction (most U.S.-designed engines rotate clockwise when viewed from the rear) and both engines develop an equal amount of thrust, the asymmetric propeller thrust, or “P-factor,” results in a center of thrust at the right side of each engine. The turning (or yawing) force of the right engine is greater than the left engine because the center of thrust is much farther away from the centerline of the fuselage; it has a longer arm. Thus, when the right engine is operative and the left engine is inoperative, the turning (or yawing) force is greater than with a good left engine and an inoperative right engine. Directional control may be difficult when the left (or critical) engine is suddenly inoperative. Answer (B) is incorrect. The critical engine of a twin-engine airplane is the one with the center of thrust closer to the centerline of the fuselage (propellers rotate in same direction), not one designated by the manufacturer. Answer (C) is incorrect. The critical engine is the one with the center of thrust closer to, not farther from, the centerline of the fuselage.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which engine is the “critical” engine of a twin-engine airplane?

choices.text: The engine whose failure has the most adverse effect on directional control.
The engine whose failure has the least adverse effect on directional control.
The engine that is operating when used by the manufacturer to determine VMC.

questions.explanation: On twins with each engine rotating in conventional, clockwise rotation as viewed from the pilot’s seat, the “critical” engine will be the left engine. The descending propeller blade of each engine will produce greater thrust (P-factor) than the ascending blade when the airplane is operated under power and at positive angles of attack. The descending propeller blade of the right engine is also a greater distance from the center of gravity and therefore has a longer moment arm than the descending propeller blade of the left engine. As a result, failure of the left engine will result in the most asymmetrical thrust (adverse yaw). Answer (B) is incorrect. The “critical” engine of a twin-engine airplane is the one whose failure has the most, not least, adverse effect on directional control. Answer (C) is incorrect. The “critical” engine is the engine whose failure will have the most adverse effect on directional control, not the engine that is operating.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: In a light, twin-engine airplane with one engine inoperative, when is it acceptable to allow the ball of a slip-skid indicator to be deflected outside the reference lines?

choices.text: When practicing imminent stalls in a banked attitude of over 60°.
While maneuvering at minimum controllable airspeed or less to avoid overbanking.
When operating at any airspeed of VMC or greater with only enough deflection to zero the side slip.

questions.explanation: Flight tests have shown that holding the ball of the turn coordinator in the center while maintaining heading with wings level increases VMC as much as 20 kt. due to increased drag. Banking into the operative engine sufficiently to achieve zero sideslip (usually 5° or less) reduces VMC and ensures that the airplane will be in a minimum drag configuration for best climb performance. Engine-out flight with the ball centered is never advisable. Answer (A) is incorrect. Stalls should never be practiced with one engine inoperative. Answer (B) is incorrect. With a 5° bank toward the good engine and the ball deflected toward the good engine, the airplane will be in a zero sideslip. There is no tendency for overbanking.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which condition has the effect of reducing critical engine failure speed?

choices.text: Slush on the runway or inoperative antiskid.

questions.explanation: Slush on the runway may dictate adjustments, such as a reduction in critical engine failure speed (V1), an increase in required runway length, or a penalty in runway limited weight. An inoperative antiskid system may have the same requirements according to the airplane flight manual or company operations manual. Answer (B) is incorrect. Low gross weight may allow an increase in critical engine failure speed. Answer (C) is incorrect. An increase in density altitude requires a higher takeoff velocity (TAS) and critical engine failure speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the safest and most efficient takeoff and initial climb procedure in a light, twin-engine airplane? Accelerate to

choices.text: Best engine-out, rate-of-climb airspeed while on the ground, then lift off and climb at that speed.
VMC, then lift off at that speed and climb at maximum angle-of-climb airspeed.
An airspeed slightly above VMC, then lift off and climb at the best rate-of-climb airspeed.

questions.explanation: On normal takeoffs, liftoff should never take place until the airspeed reaches and exceeds VMC. The FAA recommends VMC 5 kt. before liftoff. The safest and most efficient climb procedure is one in which the airplane leaves the ground slightly above VMC, accelerates to VY (best rate of climb), and climbs at VY for both engines, not single-engine. Answer (A) is incorrect. Liftoff should occur slightly above VMC, and the climb should be at the best rate-of-climb airspeed for both engines, not for an engine out. Answer (B) is incorrect. Liftoff should occur slightly above VMC, and the climb should be at the best rate, not angle, of climb.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: If an engine failure occurs at an altitude above single-engine ceiling, what airspeed should be maintained?
questions.explanation: When an engine failure occurs at an altitude above the single-engine ceiling, altitude will be lost. In an airplane not capable of maintaining altitude with an engine inoperative under existing circumstances, the airspeed should be maintained at VYSE so as to conserve altitude as long as possible. Answer (A) is incorrect. VYSE should be maintained, not the minimum controllable airspeed. Answer (C) is incorrect. The best rate-, not angle-, of-climb airspeed should be maintained.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What procedure is recommended for an engine-out approach and landing?

choices.text: The flightpath and procedures should be almost identical to a normal approach and landing.
The altitude and airspeed should be considerably higher than normal throughout the approach.
A normal approach, except do not extend the landing gear or flaps until over the runway threshold.

questions.explanation: In most light twins, a single-engine approach can be accomplished with the flight path and procedures almost identical to a normal approach and landing. However, neither full flaps nor the landing gear should be extended until the landing is assured. Answer (B) is incorrect. Higher altitude and airspeed result in floating, and unnecessary runway use should be avoided. Answer (C) is incorrect. Landing gear and full flaps should be extended when the landing is ensured, not over the runway threshold.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which part(s) in the turbojet engine is subjected to the high temperatures and severe centrifugal forces?
questions.explanation: The turbine wheel is a dynamically balanced unit consisting of blades attached to a rotating disk. The disk, in turn, is attached to the main power transmitting shaft of the engine. The jet gases leaving the turbine nozzle vanes act on the blades of the turbine wheel, causing the assembly to rotate at a very high rate of speed. The high rotational speed imposes severe centrifugal loads on the turbine wheel, and at the same time the elevated temperatures result in a lowering of the strength of the material. Consequently, the engine speed and temperature must be controlled to keep turbine operation within safe limits. Answer (B) is incorrect. The turbine vanes are not subjected to centrifugal force. Answer (C) is incorrect. The compressor rotor(s) or impeller(s) are not subjected to high temperatures.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which place in the turbojet engine is subjected to the highest temperature?
questions.explanation: There is a relatively slow rise in temperature as the air passes through the compressor inlet to the compressor discharge. The air is discharged into the combustion chamber. At the front of the combustion chamber are the fuel spray nozzles. The temperature increases rapidly in the combustion chamber and is cooled by a secondary airflow. The turbine inlet is subjected to the highest temperature in the turbojet engine. High-temperature, high-energy combustion gas is delivered through the turbine inlet from the combustion chamber. The temperature decreases through the turbine and exhaust nozzle. Answer (A) is incorrect. The compressor discharge has a relatively low, not high, temperature in the turbojet engine. Answer (B) is incorrect. The fuel spray nozzles are located in front of the combustion chamber and are not subjected to the highest temperature.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The most important restriction to the operation of turbojet or turboprop engines is
questions.explanation: The operating characteristics of the turbojet or turboprop engine provide various operating limitations. Limiting exhaust gas temperature is the most important restriction to the operation of the turbojet or turboprop engine. Answer (A) is incorrect. The turbine section is the most critical element of the turbojet engine. Temperature control is more restrictive than turbine speed, which may operate above 10,000 RPM continuously. Answer (C) is incorrect. Torque is a performance measure used on turbopropeller airplanes but is not generally applicable to turbojet engines. The most important restriction is temperature, even though, in cooler weather, a torque limitation may be reached before the temperature limitation in a turbopropeller airplane.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect would a change in ambient temperature or air density have on gas-turbine-engine performance?

choices.text: As air density decreases, thrust increases.

questions.explanation: A high ambient air temperature at a given pressure altitude relates to a high density altitude or a decrease in air density. Thrust is reduced because of low air density and low mass flow. Also, thrust and fuel flow are reduced further because of high compressor inlet temperature. Answer (A) is incorrect. As air density decreases, thrust decreases, not increases. Answer (B) is incorrect. Thrust decreases, not increases, with an increase in temperature.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect, if any, does high ambient temperature have upon the thrust output of a turbine engine?

choices.text: Thrust will be reduced due to the decrease in air density.
Thrust will remain the same, but turbine temperature will be higher.
Thrust will be higher because more heat energy is extracted from the hotter air.

questions.explanation: A high ambient temperature at a given pressure altitude relates to a high density altitude or a decrease in air density. Thrust is reduced because of the low air density and low mass flow. Also, thrust and fuel flow are reduced further because of high compressor inlet temperature. Answer (B) is incorrect. The compressor inlet, not turbine, temperature will increase at high ambient temperature. Answer (C) is incorrect. Thrust is reduced, not increased, because the hotter air is less dense, with a low mass flow.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: As outside air pressure decreases, thrust output will

choices.text: increase due to greater efficiency of jet aircraft in thin air.
remain the same since compression of inlet air will compensate for any decrease in air pressure.
decrease due to higher density altitude.

questions.explanation: Altitude is one factor that strongly affects the performance of the turbojet engine. An increase in altitude produces a decrease in density and pressure. This high density altitude causes a decrease in the engine air mass flow and, thus, a decrease in thrust output. Answer (A) is incorrect. Thrust output decreases, not increases, with a decrease in air pressure. Answer (B) is incorrect. The compression of inlet air does not compensate for the low air mass flow caused by higher density altitudes.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Equivalent shaft horsepower (ESHP) of a turboprop engine is a measure of
questions.explanation: In addition to providing jet thrust, the turboprop engine requires additional turbine stages to continue the expansion of gases in the turbine section and to extract a very large percent of the exhaust gas energy as shaft power. The turboprop is primarily a power-producing machine, and the jet thrust is a small amount of the output propulsive power. The turboprop engine is rated by ESHP, which is a measure of shaft horsepower and jet thrust. Answer (A) is incorrect. ESHP is a measure of power, not temperature. Answer (C) is incorrect. Propeller thrust is not a measurement of ESHP.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect will an increase in altitude have upon the available equivalent shaft horsepower (ESHP) of a turboprop engine?

choices.text: Lower air density and engine mass flow will cause a decrease in power.
Higher propeller efficiency will cause an increase in usable power (ESHP) and thrust.
Power will remain the same but propeller efficiency will decrease.

questions.explanation: The ESHP will vary with altitude in a manner similar to the thrust output of the turbojet because the higher altitude produces much lower density and engine mass flow. Answer (B) is incorrect. Propeller efficiency decreases, not increases, with an increase in altitude. Answer (C) is incorrect. Power will decrease, not remain the same, with an increase in altitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Minimum specific fuel consumption of the turboprop engine is normally available in which altitude range?
questions.explanation: The minimum specific fuel consumption is obtained at relatively high power setting and high altitudes. The low inlet air temperature reduces the specific fuel consumption, and the lowest is obtained near altitudes of 25,000 to 35,000 ft. (or to the tropopause). Answer (A) is incorrect. The altitude range is from 25,000 to 35,000 ft., not 10,000 to 25,000 ft. Answer (C) is incorrect. The tropopause is the highest, not lowest, altitude range for minimum specific fuel consumption.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A rule of thumb states that a 1,000 foot increase in density altitude for a turbojet with a high thrust-to-weight ratio will cause a takeoff distance increase of
questions.explanation: Some appropriate rules of thumb may be derived to illustrate the differences between various airplane types. A 1,000-foot increase in density altitude will cause approximately a 7% increase in takeoff distance for a turbojet with high thrust-to-weight ratio. Answer (B) is incorrect. At a given gross weight, every 1,000-foot increase in density altitude results in a 5% increase in landing distance, not a decrease in takeoff distance. Each 1% excess in velocity incurs approximately 2% additional takeoff distance. Answer (C) is incorrect. The approximate increase in takeoff distance for a turbojet with low thrust-to-weight ratio is 2%.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: For an airplane with a relatively high thrust-to-weight ratio, a 10% increase in takeoff gross weight would result in a takeoff distance increase of approximately
questions.explanation: The takeoff distance will vary at least as the square of the gross weight varies. For example, a 10% increase in takeoff gross weight would cause a 5% increase in takeoff velocity, at least a 9% decrease in acceleration, and at least a 21% increase in takeoff distance. For the airplane with a high thrust-to-weight ratio, the increase in takeoff distance would be approximately 21% to 22%. Answer (A) is incorrect. An increase of 30% or more would require approximately a 15% increase in takeoff gross weight. Answer (C) is incorrect. An increase of 11% would require approximately 5% increase in takeoff gross weight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: High Density altitude conditions result in
questions.explanation: The difference you will see at high density altitude (DA) is your true airspeed (TAS) and, with no wind, ground speed will be higher than at sea level for the same indicated airspeed. For example, you when you rotate at 67 knots indicated, at sea level, you will be at 67 knots TAS. At 8,000 ft. density altitude, however, 67 KIAS is 76 KTAS. With no wind, you’ll be rotating 9 knots faster ground speed. Answer (B) is incorrect. Indicated airspeeds would be the same at high or low density altitudes. Answer (C) is incorrect. Lower true airspeeds will be at lower density altitudes.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Aerodynamic studies prove

choices.text: turbojet powered airplanes and reciprocating engine powered are airplanes equally sensitive to density altitude.
turbojet powered airplanes are more sensitive to density altitude than reciprocating engine powered airplanes.
reciprocating engine powered airplanes are more sensitive to density altitude than turbojet powered airplanes.

questions.explanation: The turbojet airplane is much more sensitive to density altitude than the reciprocating powered airplane because the effect of density altitude on powerplant thrust depends much on the type of powerplant. An increase in altitude above standard sea level will bring an immediate decrease in power output for the unsupercharged or the turbojet and turboprop engines. Answer (A) is incorrect. The effect of density altitude on powerplant thrust depends much on the type of powerplant. A reciprocating engine airplane is less sensitive to density altitude than a turbojet because reciprocating engines can be supercharged. Answer (C) is incorrect. The effect of density altitude on powerplant thrust depends much on the type of powerplant. A reciprocating engine airplane is less sensitive to density altitude than a turbojet because reciprocating engines can be supercharged. Thus, a 1,000-ft. increase in density altitude will cause an approximate 3.5% increase in takeoff distance for the supercharged reciprocating airplane when below critical altitude, while it could cause upwards of 7% for a turbojet.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A turboprop engine

choices.text: has superior performance during takeoff than a turbojet.
has low propulsive efficiency and low thrust available.

questions.explanation: The performance of the turboprop illustrates the typical advantages of the propeller-engine combination. Higher propulsive efficiency combined with high thrust and low speeds provides superior range, endurance, and takeoff performance relative to the turbojet. Answer (A) is incorrect. All propeller equipped powerplants have nearly constant power with speed unlike a turbojet which decreases slightly. Answer (C) is incorrect. Turboprop engines have higher propulsive efficiency and high thrust, along with low speeds. They provide range, endurance, and takeoff performance superior to a turbojet.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What characterizes a transient compressor stall?

choices.text: Loud, steady roar accompanied by heavy shuddering.
Sudden loss of thrust accompanied by a loud whine. ⑧
Intermittent “bang,” as backfires and flow reversals take place.

questions.explanation: As a compressor stall occurs, the pressure rises and the compressor does not furnish discharge at a pressure equal to the combustion chamber pressure. As a result, a flow reversal or backfire takes place. If the stall is transient and intermittent, the indication will be the intermittent “bang” as backfire and flow reversal take place. Answer (A) is incorrect. This describes a developed and steady stall, not a transient stall. Answer (B) is incorrect. A transient stall is characterized by an intermittent “bang,” not a loud whine.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What indicates that a compressor stall has developed and become steady? g

choices.text: Complete loss of power with severe reduction in airspeed.

questions.explanation: As a compressor stall occurs, the pressure rises and the compressor does not furnish discharge at a pressure equal to the combustion chamber pressure. As a result, a flow reversal or backfire takes place. If the stall develops and becomes steady, strong vibrations and a loud roar develop from the continuous flow reversal. Answer (B) is incorrect. An occasional loud “bang” and flow reversal describe an indication of a transient stall, not a stall that has developed and become steady. Answer (C) is incorrect. A compressor stall will not cause a complete loss of power.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which type of compressor stall has the greatest potential for severe engine damage?
questions.explanation: In a steady compressor stall, strong vibrations and a loud roar develop from the continuous flow reversal. The increase in compressor power required tends to reduce RPM, and the reduced airflow and increased fuel flow cause a rapid, immediate rise in exhaust gas temperature. The possibility of engine damage is immediate with the steady stall. Answer (A) is incorrect. An intermittent “backfire” stall does not have as great a potential for severe engine damage as a steady stall. Answer (B) is incorrect. A transient “backfire” stall does not have as great a potential for severe engine damage as a steady stall.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What recovery would be appropriate in the event of compressor stall?

choices.text: Reduce the throttle and then rapidly advance the throttle to decrease the angle of attack on the compressor blades, creating more airflow. &
Reduce the throttle and then slowly advance the throttle again and decrease the aircraft’s angle of attack.
Advance the throttle slowly to increase airflow and decrease the angle of attack on one or more compressor blades.

questions.explanation: To recover from a compressor stall, the pilot should reduce the throttle, decrease the aircraft’s angle of attack, and increase airspeed. These steps will allow the compressor blades to recover from the stall that precipitated the issue. Answer (A) is incorrect. The angle of attack of the compressor blades is a result of the vector caused by the inlet air velocity and the rotational velocity of the blades. Recovery from a compressor stall should be accomplished by quickly reducing power, decreasing the aircraft’s angle of attack, and increasing airspeed. Answer (C) is incorrect. It is necessary to reduce the aircraft’s angle of attack and increase airspeed to recover from a compressor stall. It is not possible for the pilot to decrease the angle of attack on individual compressor blades.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What limits turbine engines from developing compressor stalls?
questions.explanation: To prevent compressor stalls, compressor bleed valves are contained in the system to restrict the engine until it is at an rpm that allows it to respond to a rapid acceleration demand without distress. Answer (A) is incorrect. Deice valves and heated fuel do not contribute to the prevention of compressor stalls in turbine engines. Answer (C) is incorrect. The TKS system is an anti-icing system that prevents ice from building up on the aircraft. It does not play a role in the prevention of compressor stalls.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What prevents turbine engines from developing compressor stalls?
questions.explanation: The compressor bleed valves and the fuel nozzle and spray patterns along with their governors help restrict the fuel flow and chamber pressure until the engine RPM is at acceptable tolerances. Answer (A) is incorrect. The TKS system is a chemical deicing system that is primarily used as an anti-icing system. It does not reduce or prevent compressor stalls. Answer (C) is incorrect. If warm fuel is flown to high altitudes, the fuel will cool and may cause ice crystals. Fuel heat will help eliminate these crystals, and that reduces the possibility of flameouts, but does not directly affect compressor stalls. The compressor bleed valves help prevent turbine engines from developing stalls.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: At what Mach range does the subsonic flight range normally occur?
questions.explanation: Since there is a possibility of having both subsonic and supersonic flows existing on the aircraft, it is convenient to define certain regimes of flight. Subsonic flight range occurs in Mach numbers below 0.75. Answer (B) is incorrect. From 0.75 to 1.20 Mach is the transonic, not subsonic, flight regime. Answer (C) is incorrect. From 1.20 to 2.50 Mach is part of the supersonic, not subsonic, flight regime.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Within what Mach range does transonic flight regimes usually occur?
questions.explanation: Since there is a possibility of having both subsonic and supersonic flows existing on the aircraft, it is convenient to define certain regimes of flight. Transonic flight regimes occur in Mach numbers from 0.75 to 1.20. Answer (A) is incorrect. Mach 0.50 to 0.75 is part of the subsonic, not transonic, flight regime. Answer (C) is incorrect. Mach 1.20 to 2.50 is part of the supersonic, not transonic, flight regime.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the free stream Mach number which produces first evidence of local sonic flow?
questions.explanation: By definition, critical Mach number is the “free stream Mach number which produces first evidence of local sonic flow.” Therefore, shock waves, buffet, airflow separation, etc., take place above critical Mach number. Answer (A) is incorrect. The free stream Mach number that produces first evidence of local sonic flow is the critical, not supersonic, Mach number. Answer (B) is incorrect. The free stream Mach number that produces first evidence of local sonic flow is the critical, not transonic, Mach number.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the highest speed possible without supersonic flow over the wing?
questions.explanation: The highest speed possible without supersonic flow over the wing is termed the critical Mach number. Answer (A) is incorrect. The initial buffet speed occurs above the critical Mach number when an area of supersonic flow is created over the wing. Answer (C) is incorrect. The critical Mach number, not the transonic index, is the highest speed possible without supersonic flow over the wing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the movement of the center of pressure when the wingtips of a sweptwing airplane are shock-stalled first?
questions.explanation: On a sweptwing airplane, the wing center of pressure shifts when the airplane is shock-stalled. On a sweptwing airplane when the wingtips are shock-stalled first, the center of pressure will move forward and inward. Answer (A) is incorrect. When the wingtips are shock-stalled first, the center of pressure moves forward, not aft. Answer (C) is incorrect. When the wingtips are shock-stalled first, the center of pressure moves inward, not outward.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the result of a shock-induced separation of airflow occurring symmetrically near the wing root of a sweptwing aircraft?

choices.text: A high-speed stall and sudden pitchup.

questions.explanation: When airflow separation occurs on the wing due to shock wave formation, there will be a loss of lift and a subsequent loss of downwash aft of the affected area. If the shock-induced separation occurs symmetrically near the wing root, a decrease in downwash behind this area is caused by a loss of lift. A decrease in downwash on the horizontal tail will create a diving moment and the aircraft will perform a “Mach tuck.” Answer (A) is incorrect. There is a sudden pitch down, not up, when a shock-induced separation of airflow occurs symmetrically near the wing root of a sweptwing aircraft. Answer (C) is incorrect. There is a diving moment, not severe porpoising, when a shock-induced separation of airflow occurs symmetrically near the wing root of a sweptwing aircraft.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the principal advantage of a sweepback design wing over a straightwing design?

choices.text: The critical Mach number will increase significantly.
Sweepback will increase changes in the magnitude of force coefficients due to compressibility.
Sweepback will accelerate the onset of compressibility effect.

questions.explanation: The sweep of a surface produces a beneficial effect in high-speed flight since higher flight speeds may be obtained before components of speed perpendicular to the leading edge produce critical conditions on the wing. One of the most important advantages of a sweepback wing design is an increase in the critical Mach number. Answer (B) is incorrect. Sweepback will reduce, not increase, changes in the magnitude of force coefficients due to compressibility. Answer (C) is incorrect. Sweepback will delay, not accelerate, the onset of compressibility effect.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is one disadvantage of a sweptwing design?

choices.text: The wing root stalls prior to the wingtip section.
The wingtip section stalls prior to the wing root.
Severe pitchdown moment when the center of pressure shifts forward.

questions.explanation: The use of a swept wing design produces certain disadvantages that are important from the standpoint of both airplane design and flight operations. One disadvantage is that, when sweepback is combined with taper, there is an extremely powerful tendency for the wingtip section to stall prior to the wing root. Answer (A) is incorrect. A swept wing design has a tendency for the wingtip, not wing root, to stall first. Answer (C) is incorrect. When the center of pressure shifts forward, there is a pitch up, not down, moment.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Swept wings

choices.text: increases the speed of sound quotient.

questions.explanation: Swept wings can produce major effects on the aerodynamic characteristics. One of the most important advantages of the sweep is an increase in critical Mach number, which will delay the onset of compressibility effects at which drag will increase dramatically. Answer (A) is incorrect. Improved specific fuel consumption is a byproduct of the swept wings, however the most important advantage of the swept wing is the increase in the critical Mach number, which delays the onset of compressibility effects. Answer (C) is incorrect. The Mach number typically exceeds the critical Mach number by 5-10%. At that speed the airflow is induced by a shockwave (the speed of sound). The airflow on a swept wing causes the airflow to hit the wing leading edge at an angle less than 90°, thus delaying the airflow separation and reducing the onset of a shockwave rather than increasing it.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A jet airplane operating at a cruise speed of .75 Mach with outside air temperature of – 42 degrees C has a true airspeed of
