Find the Mach number on the “minutes” scale, and read TAS above on “miles” scale, or 446 kt. Answer (A) is incorrect. A TAS of 429 kt. would be correct for an OAT of –60°C. Answer (C) is incorrect. A TAS of 455 kt. would be correct for an OAT of –35°C.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: For significant benefit, wing sweep must be at least

choices.text: 55° or more to substantially delay compressibility effects.

questions.explanation: Sweepback will reduce the magnitude of change in the aerodynamic force coefficients due to compressibility. The use of sweepback on a transonic aircraft will reduce and delay the drag rise and preserve the maneuverability of the aircraft in transonic flight. If sweepback is to be used at all at least 30° to 35° must be used to produce any significant benefit. Answer (B) is incorrect. The benefits of sweepback begin at 30° to 35° of sweep. Answer (C) is incorrect. The benefits of sweepback begin at 30° to 35° of sweep. There are stability issues with sweepback wings of 55° or more.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: “Drag rise” usually occurs

choices.text: 5 to 10% above the critical Mach number.
2 to 3% above the critical Mach number.

questions.explanation: The Mach number which produces a sharp change in the drag coefficient is termed force divergence or drag rise. Drag rise usually occurs 5% to 10% above the critical Mach number. Answer (B) is incorrect. A 2% to 3% above critical Mach number would be the beginning of supersonic flow and would not produce drag rise. Answer (C) is incorrect. The Mach convergence number is at Mach 1, not beyond it. Drag rise is beyond Mach 1.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Above the critical Mach number, you can expect
questions.explanation: Aircraft above the critical Mach number can cause airflow separation. Answer (A) is incorrect. All components of the aircraft are affected by compressibility in a manner somewhat similar to that of basic airfoil. The tail, fuselage, nacelles, etc., and the effect of the interference between the various surfaces of the aircraft must be considered. Aircraft above the critical Mach number should always expect some sort of airflow separation which may result in rudder control vibrations. Answer (B) is incorrect. All components of the aircraft are affected by compressibility in a manner somewhat similar to that of basic airfoil. The tail, fuselage, nacelles, etc. and the effect of the interference between the various surfaces of the aircraft must be considered. Aircraft above the critical Mach number should always expect some sort of airflow separation which may result in wingtip flutter.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: As flight approaches the speed of sound,

choices.text: all changes in velocity and pressure will take place quite suddenly.
the airflow ahead of the aircraft is aggressively influenced and is forced out of the way.
all changes in velocity and pressure will take place quite slowly.

questions.explanation: The airflow ahead of the object is not influenced until the air particles are suddenly forced out of the way by the object quite sharply and suddenly as flight approaches the speed of sound. Answer (B) is incorrect. As the flight speed nears the speed of sound, a compression wave will form at the leading edge. The airflow ahead of the aircraft is not influenced or moved out of the way. The air velocity and pressure change very quickly. Answer (C) is incorrect. All changes in velocity and pressure will take place quite suddenly when speeds are approaching the speed of sound.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A “buzz” felt in the flight controls in cruise flight might be an indication of
questions.explanation: “Drag rise” is associated with buffet, trim and stability changes and a decrease in control surface effectiveness. Aileron, rudder, and elevator surfaces subjected to this buffet may “buzz.” Answer (B) is incorrect. The Critical Mach Tuck, or “tuck under,” may result from drag rise, which causes a decrease in downwash on the horizontal tail. Answer (C) is incorrect. “Drag rise,” not “force rise,” may result in a “buzz,” which is a result of the critical Mach number being exceeded.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: “Drag divergence” usually occurs

choices.text: 5% to 10% above the critical Mach number.
2% to 3% above the critical Mach number.

questions.explanation: The Mach number that produces a sharp change in the drag coefficient is termed drag divergence or drag rise. Drag rise usually occurs 5% to 10% above the critical Mach number. Answer (B) is incorrect. The Mach number that produces a sharp change in the drag coefficient is termed drag divergence or drag rise. A level of 2% to 3% above the critical Mach number is not enough to produce drag divergence. Answer (C) is incorrect. The Mach convergence number is a Mach number and a convergence trend.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Trim and stability changes in cruise

choices.text: may be caused by drag divergence effects.
are caused by the “tuck under” effect.
may be caused by drag convergence effects.

questions.explanation: Airflow separation can create significant variations in the aerodynamic forces. At speeds over the critical Mach number, trim and stability changes along with a decrease in control effectiveness may occur. These changes are caused by drag divergence effects. Answer (B) is incorrect. Trim and stability changes may cause “tuck under” (Mach tuck) if not corrected. Trim and stability changes are usually what cause Mach tuck. Answer (C) is incorrect. Drag divergence, not convergence, effects may be a cause of trim and stability changes in cruise.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Transonic airflow across an aircraft

choices.text: may be partly subsonic and partly supersonic.

questions.explanation: In the transonic regime, it is very probable that flow on the aircraft components may be partly subsonic and partly supersonic. Answer (B) is incorrect. Transonic airflow may be partly subsonic and partly supersonic. Answer (C) is incorrect. The principal differences between subsonic and supersonic flow are the compressibility effects.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The number which produces a sharp change in the drag coefficient is the
questions.explanation: The Mach number that produces a sharp change in the drag coefficient is termed drag divergence, force divergence, or drag rise. Drag rise usually occurs 5% to 10% above the critical Mach number. Answer (B) is incorrect. The critical Mach number is the free stream Mach number, which produces first evidence of local sonic flow. Answer (C) is incorrect. The tuck Mach number refers to the speed at which the nose will pitch down due to the center of lift moving aft over the wing. This movement is created by local sonic flows over the wing.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A jet airplane operating at cruise of .82 Mach with an OAT of -44°C has a true airspeed of
questions.explanation: Using an E6B flight computer, rotate the right inner wheel cutout until the Mach number index is seen. Line the arrow of the Mach number index with the temperature -44°C. Find the 82 on the minute scale on the outer portion of the inner wheel. Above the 82 on the “miles” scale is a little past 48 (48.8). Common sense tells us it cannot be 48.8 knots, but can be 488 knots. The closest answer to the FAA’s answers is 486 knots TAS. Answer (A) is incorrect. Mach .79 would be about 477 knots true airspeed with -44°C. Answer (C) is incorrect. Mach .83 would be about 494 knots true airspeed with -44°C.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What could be one result of exceeding critical Mach number?
questions.explanation: Critical Mach number is the boundary between subsonic and transonic flight and is largely dependent on the wing and airfoil design. Critical Mach number is an important point in transonic flight. When shock waves form on the aircraft, airflow separation, followed by buffet and aircraft control difficulties, can occur. Answer (A) is incorrect. Propeller slippage is not associated with flight near the critical Mach speed. Rather, it has to do with the loss in efficiency inherent in the operation of any propeller-driven aircraft, particularly with fixed-pitch propellers. Answer (B) is incorrect. Critical Mach number is the highest flight speed possible without supersonic flow. Accelerating past critical Mach is associated with a large increase in drag, not a reduction in drag. This is due to the initial formation of a weak shock wave on the wing, creating a barrier to the oncoming airflow.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How should thrust reversers be applied to reduce landing distance for turbojet aircraft?
questions.explanation: Reverse thrust of turbojet engines will usually employ some form of vanes, buckets, or clamshells in the exhaust to turn or direct the exhaust gases forward. Reverse thrust must be applied immediately after ground contact for maximum effectiveness in reducing landing distance. Answer (B) is incorrect. Thrust reversers should be applied immediately after, not prior to, ground contact to reduce landing distance. Answer (C) is incorrect. Thrust reversers should be applied immediately after ground contact, not after applying maximum wheel braking, to reduce landing distance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How should reverse thrust propellers be used during landing for maximum effectiveness in stopping?

choices.text: Gradually increase reverse power to maximum as rollout speed decreases.
Use maximum reverse power as soon as possible after touchdown.
Select reverse-pitch after landing and use idle power setting of the engines.

questions.explanation: Reverse thrust of propellers is obtained by rotating the blade angle well below the low pitch stop and applying engine power. The action is to extract a large amount of momentum from the airstream and create negative thrust. Maximum effectiveness is achieved by use of maximum reverse power immediately after the airplane is in contact with the runway. Answer (A) is incorrect. Maximum effectiveness is achieved by use of maximum reverse power as soon as possible after touchdown, not as the rollout speed decreases. Answer (C) is incorrect. Power should be at maximum, not idle, to add to drag and braking friction to increase the net retarding force.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: A definition of the term “viscous hydroplaning” is where

choices.text: the airplane rides on standing water.
a film of moisture covers the painted or rubber-coated portion of the runway.
the tires of the airplane are actually riding on a mixture of steam and melted rubber.

questions.explanation: Viscous hydroplaning can occur on a thin film of water if it covers the painted or rubber-coated portion of the runway. Answer (A) is incorrect. Dynamic hydroplaning occurs when the airplane tires ride on standing water. Answer (C) is incorrect. Reverted rubber hydroplaning occurs when the tires of the airplane are actually riding on a mixture of steam and melted rubber.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Compared to dynamic hydroplaning, at what speed does viscous hydroplaning occur when landing on a smooth, wet runway?

choices.text: At approximately 2.0 times the speed that dynamic hydroplaning occurs.
At a lower speed than dynamic hydroplaning.
At the same speed as dynamic hydroplaning.

questions.explanation: Viscous hydroplaning may occur at lower speeds and at lower water depths than dynamic hydroplaning. Answer (A) is incorrect. Dynamic hydroplaning usually occurs at a higher speed than viscous hydroplaning. Answer (C) is incorrect. Viscous hydroplaning often occurs on smooth runway pavements or where rubber deposits are present, usually in the touchdown area where a thin film of water can significantly reduce the coefficient of friction. This usually occurs at a speed lower than dynamic hydroplaning.

questions.question: At what minimum speed will dynamic hydroplaning begin if a tire has an air pressure of 70 PSI?
questions.explanation: The minimum speed in knots for dynamic hydroplaning can be calculated by the following formula: Answer (A) is incorrect. Hydroplaning will occur at 85 kt. with a tire pressure of 95 PSI. Answer (B) is incorrect. Hydroplaning will occur at 80 kt. with a tire pressure of 84 PSI.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which term describes the hydroplaning which occurs when an airplane’s tire is effectively held off a smooth runway surface by steam generated by friction?
questions.explanation: Reverted rubber hydroplaning is the result of a locked wheel skid in which reverted rubber becomes a barrier between the tire and the runway. Steam generated by the heat of friction will hold the wheel off a smooth runway surface. Answer (B) is incorrect. Dynamic hydroplaning occurs when there is standing water or slush on the runway that forms a wedge that lifts the tire away from contact with the runway surface. Answer (C) is incorrect. Viscous hydroplaning occurs on a thin film of water on a smooth (e.g., painted or rubber coated) runway surface.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the best method of speed reduction if hydroplaning is experienced on landing?

choices.text: Apply full main wheel braking only.
Apply nosewheel and main wheel braking alternately and abruptly.
Apply aerodynamic braking to the fullest advantage.

questions.explanation: During hydroplaning, the tire(s) is(are) not in contact with the runway surface, so there is no friction, and application of the brakes would do nothing. Aerodynamic braking must be used to its fullest advantage. Answer (A) is incorrect. Applying full main wheel braking may increase or compound the problems associated with hydroplaning. If any brakes are used, a pumping or modulating motion like an antiskid system can be used. Aerodynamic braking is recommended. Answer (B) is incorrect. Abrupt use of either the nosewheel or the mainwheel brakes will lock the wheels and compound the problem.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Under what conditions might a pilot expect the possibility of hydroplaning?

choices.text: When landing on a wet runway that is covered in rubber from previous landings.
When departing a grooved runway with less than a thousandth of an inch of water.
When the adiabatic lapse rate is high, and steam is rising from the landing surface.

questions.explanation: Wet runways with standing water coupled with rubber deposits would present friction coefficients conducive to hydroplaning. Answer (B) is incorrect. Grooved runways offer higher friction capability, and the standing water present is less than that required to induce hydroplaning. Answer (C) is incorrect. Reverted rubber hydroplaning occurs when an airplane’s tires are effectively held off the smooth runway surface by steam generated by friction, not by steam from a humid atmosphere.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What effect, if any, will landing at a higher-than-recommended touchdown speed have on hydroplaning?

choices.text: No effect on hydroplaning, but increases landing roll.
Reduces hydroplaning potential if heavy braking is applied.
Increases hydroplaning potential regardless of braking.

questions.explanation: Landing at a higher-than-recommended touchdown speed increases the hydroplaning potential because the wings provide lift and reduce the contact between the tires and the runway, allowing a layer of water to form between the tire and the runway. Answer (A) is incorrect. Landing at a higher airspeed increases the hydroplaning potential. Answer (B) is incorrect. Landing at a higher airspeed increases, not reduces, the hydroplaning potential, regardless of braking.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is an effect of ice, snow, or frost formation on an airplane?

choices.text: Decreased angle of attack for stalls.

questions.explanation: When ice, snow, or particularly frost forms on the upper surface of a wing, it provides a surface texture of considerable roughness. The increase in surface roughness increases skin friction drag and reduces the kinetic energy of the boundary layer, causing incipient stalling of the wing; i.e., separation will occur at angles of attack lower than for the clean, smooth wing. In some aircraft, stall will occur prior to activation of stall warning devices. Answer (A) is incorrect. The formation of ice, snow, or frost on the wings of an aircraft increases, not decreases, stall speed. Answer (B) is incorrect. The formation of ice, snow, or frost on the wings of some aircraft may increase, not decrease, pitchup tendencies.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is an effect of ice, snow, or frost formation on an airplane?

choices.text: Increased angle of attack for stalls.

questions.explanation: When ice, snow, or particularly frost forms on the upper surface of a wing, it provides a surface texture of considerable roughness. The increase in surface roughness increases skin friction drag and reduces the kinetic energy of the boundary layer, causing an increase in power required and stall speed. Answer (B) is incorrect. The formation of ice, snow, or frost on the wings of some aircraft may increase pitchup, not pitchdown, tendencies. Answer (C) is incorrect. The formation of ice, snow, or frost on the wings of an aircraft decreases, not increases, the angle of attack for stalls. In some aircraft, stall will occur prior to activation of stall warning devices.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The adverse effects of ice, snow, or frost on aircraft performance and flight characteristics include decreased lift and
questions.explanation: The adverse effects of ice, snow, or frost on aircraft performance and flight characteristics are generally reflected in the form of decreased lift, increased stall speed, decreased thrust, trim changes, and altered stall characteristics and handling qualities. Answer (A) is incorrect. The adverse effects of ice, snow, or frost on aircraft performance and flight characteristics include a decrease, not an increase, in thrust. Answer (B) is incorrect. The adverse effects of ice, snow, or frost on aircraft performance and flight characteristics include an increase, not a decrease, in stall speed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost having a thickness and roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of a wing can

choices.text: reduce lift by as much as 40 percent and increase drag by 30 percent.
reduce lift by as much as 30 percent and increase drag by 40 percent.
increase drag and reduce lift by as much as 40 percent.

questions.explanation: Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost formations having a thickness and surface roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of a wing can reduce wing lift by as much as 30% and increase drag by 40%. These changes in lift and drag significantly increase stall speed, reduce controllability, and alter aircraft flight characteristics. Answer (A) is incorrect. Ice, snow, or frost on the leading edge and upper surface of a wing can reduce lift by 30%, not 40%, and increase drag by 40%, not 30%. Answer (C) is incorrect. Ice, snow, or frost on the leading edge and upper surface of a wing can reduce lift by 30%, not 40%.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Freezing Point Depressant (FPD) fluids used for deicing

choices.text: are intended to provide ice protection on the ground only.
on the ground cause no performance degradation during takeoff.

questions.explanation: FPD fluids are used to aid the ground deicing process and to provide a protective film of FPD (anti-icing) to delay formations of frost, snow, or other ice until after takeoff. During flight, an aircraft’s deice/anti-ice equipment (if installed) provides ice protection. Answer (A) is incorrect. FPD fluids used during ground deicing are not intended for, and do not provide, ice protection during flight. Answer (C) is incorrect. Some large aircraft do experience performance degradation during takeoff, and on small airplanes, degradation is significant.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Freezing Point Depressant (FPD) fluids are highly soluble in water; however,

choices.text: Ice is slow to absorb it but fast to melt when in contact with FPD.
Ice absorbs it very fast but is slow to melt when in contact with it.
Ice is slow to absorb it, and to melt when in contact with it.

questions.explanation: FPD fluids are very soluble in water. However, the rate at which ice will absorb FPD or melt is very slow. Thus, ice formations adhering to a wing surface must be melted by repeated application of FPD fluids or by application of heated fluid. Answer (A) is incorrect. The rate at which ice will melt when in contact with FPD is very slow, not fast. Answer (B) is incorrect. The rate at which ice will absorb FPD is very slow, not fast.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Freezing Point Depressant (FPD) fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades

choices.text: Can increase performance and cause stalls or surges.
Could cause FPD vapors to enter the aircraft but would have no effect on engine thrust or power.
Can reduce engine performance and cause surging and/or compressor stalls.

questions.explanation: FPD fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades can reduce engine performance or cause a stall or a surge. In addition, this residue could increase the possibility of, or the quantity of, glycol vapors entering the aircraft through the engine bleed air system. Answer (A) is incorrect. FPD fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades can reduce, not increase, performance. Answer (B) is incorrect. FPD fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades can reduce, rather than have no effect on, performance.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the effect of Freezing Point Depressant (FPD) fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades?

choices.text: It could cause FPD vapors to enter the aircraft but would have no effect on engine thrust or power.
It can increase performance and cause stalls or surges.
It can reduce engine performance and cause surging and/or compressor stalls.

questions.explanation: FPD fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades can reduce engine performance and cause surging and/or compressor stalls. In addition, this residue could increase the possibility of, or the quantity of, glycol vapors entering the aircraft through the engine bleed air system. Answer (A) is incorrect. FPD fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades can reduce engine thrust or power in addition to allowing FPD vapors to enter the aircraft. Answer (B) is incorrect. FPD fluid residue on engine fan or compressor blades can reduce, not increase, engine performance and cause stalls or surges.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The practice developed and accepted by the North American air carrier industry using traditional North American fluids is to ensure that the freeze point of the remaining film is below ambient temperature by at least
questions.explanation: The practice developed and accepted by the North American air carrier industry using traditional North American fluids is to ensure that the remaining film has a freeze point of at least 20°F below ambient temperature. The remaining film should have a freeze point of at least 20°F, not 20°C, below ambient temperature.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Anti-icing fluid should provide freezing point protection to

choices.text: A freezing point no greater than 20°F below the ambient or airplane surface temperature.

questions.explanation: The practice developed and accepted by the air carrier industry is to ensure that the residual surface film of anti-icing fluid should provide freezing point protection to at least 20°F (11°C) below the colder of ambient or aircraft surface (skin) temperature. Answer (A) is incorrect. Anti-icing fluid should have a freezing point no greater than 20°F below ambient or surface temperature, whichever is lower, regardless of ambient temperature. Answer (B) is incorrect. Anti-icing fluid should have a freezing point no greater than 20°F below ambient or surface temperature, whichever is lower, regardless of outside temperature.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Snow on top of deicing or anti-icing fluids

choices.text: Need not be considered as adhering to the aircraft.
Must be considered as adhering to the aircraft.
Must be considered as adhering to the aircraft, but a safe takeoff can be made as it will blow off.

questions.explanation: Ice, snow, or frost on top of deicing or anti-icing fluids must be considered as adhering to the aircraft. Takeoff should not be attempted. Answer (A) is incorrect. Ice, snow, or frost on top of deicing or anti-icing fluids must be considered as adhering to the aircraft. Answer (C) is incorrect. Takeoff should not be attempted.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The purpose of diluting ethylene glycol deicing fluid with water in non-precipitation conditions is to

choices.text: Increase the minimum freezing point (onset of crystallization).

questions.explanation: Pure ethylene glycol will freeze at warmer temperatures than that diluted with water. For this reason, all currently available commercial and military deicing fluids contain small quantities of water. Answer (A) is incorrect. The eutectic point, or minimum freezing point (onset of crystallization), is a fixed value that occurs with a specific mixture of glycol and water for which the freezing temperature is at its lowest. Answer (C) is incorrect. The minimum freezing point (onset of crystallization), or eutectic point, is a fixed value that occurs with a specific mixture of glycol and water for which the freezing temperature is at its lowest.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the minimum glycol content of Type 1 deicing/anti-icing fluid?
questions.explanation: Type 1 deicing/anti-icing fluids in the concentrated form contain a minimum of 80% glycols and are considered “unthickened” because of their relatively low viscosity. These fluids are used for deicing or anti-icing but provide very limited anti-icing protection. Answer (A) is incorrect. The minimum glycol content of Type 1 fluid is 80%, not 30%. Answer (B) is incorrect. Fifty percent is the minimum glycol content of Type 2, not Type 1, fluid.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What is the minimum glycol content of Type 2 deicing/anti-icing fluid?
questions.explanation: Type 2 deicing/anti-icing fluids contain a minimum of 50% glycols and are considered “thickened” because of added thickening agents that enable the fluid to be deposited in a thicker film and to remain on the aircraft surfaces until the time of takeoff. These fluids are used for deicing and anti-icing, and provide greater protection than do Type 1 fluids against ice, frost, or snow formation in conditions conducive to aircraft icing on the ground. Answer (A) is incorrect. The minimum glycol content of Type 2 fluid is 50%, not 30%. Answer (C) is incorrect. Eighty percent is the minimum glycol content of Type 1, not Type 2, fluid.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which is a disadvantage of the one-step over the two-step process when deicing/anti-icing an airplane?

choices.text: More fluid is used with the one-step method when large deposits of ice and snow must be flushed off airplane surfaces.

questions.explanation: The one-step process for deicing/anti-icing an airplane consists of applying heated fluid onto the airplane surfaces to remove accumulated ice, snow, or frost and prevent their subsequent buildup. Its primary disadvantage is that, when large deposits of ice and snow must be flushed off of airplane surfaces, the total fluid usage will be greater than for a two-step process. In the two-step procedure, you may use water or a very diluted Type 1 fluid to first deice the wing and then the Type 2, thus using less fluid. Answer (A) is incorrect. The primary advantage of the one-step process is that it is quick and uncomplicated. Answer (B) is incorrect. Since the one-step process uses heated fluid, the holding time is decreased, not increased.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which procedure increases holding time when deicing/anti-icing an airplane using a two-step process?

choices.text: Heated Type 1 fluid followed by cold Type 2 fluid.
Cold Type 2 fluid followed by hot Type 2 fluid.
Heated Type 1 or 2 fluid followed by cold Type 1 fluid.

questions.explanation: The two-step process consists of separate deicing and anti-icing steps. First, a heated, diluted Type 1 fluid is applied to remove accumulated ice, snow, or frost. Then a cold, more concentrated fluid is applied. Using a Type 2 fluid for the second step increases the holding time (i.e., the time the fluid will protect the aircraft from ice, snow, and frost) significantly due to its higher viscosity. Answer (B) is incorrect. Using a heated, not cold, fluid in the first step helps melt any accumulated ice, snow, or frost, and using a cold, not hot, fluid in the second step leaves greater amounts of residual film, increasing holding time. Answer (C) is incorrect. Using a Type 2 fluid for the second step increases the holding time (i.e., the time the fluid will protect the aircraft from ice, snow, and frost) significantly due to its higher viscosity.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Which of the following will decrease the holding time during anti-icing using a two-step process?

choices.text: Increase the viscosity of Type 1 fluid.

questions.explanation: The two-step process consists of separate deicing and anti-icing steps. First, a heated, diluted Type 1 fluid is applied to remove accumulated ice, snow, or frost. Then a cold, more concentrated fluid is applied. Using a heated Type 2 fluid in the second step will leave less amounts of residual film, decreasing holding time. Answer (B) is incorrect. Decreasing the water content of the anti-icing fluid increases its viscosity, which will increase, not decrease, holding time. Answer (C) is incorrect. Increasing the viscosity of Type 1 fluid requires lowering its temperature. This will increase, not decrease, holding time because it will leave greater amounts of residual film.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What should the deice/anti-ice fluid temperature be during the last step of a two-phase process?
questions.explanation: The two-step process consists of separate deicing and anti-icing steps. First, a heated, diluted Type 1 fluid is applied to remove accumulated ice, snow, or frost. Then a cold, more concentrated fluid is applied. Using a cold fluid in the second step will leave greater amounts of residual film, increasing the effectiveness of the deice/anti-ice fluid. Answer (A) is incorrect. Using a cold, not hot, fluid in the second step will leave greater amounts of residual film, increasing the effectiveness of the deice/anti-ice fluid. Answer (B) is incorrect. Using a cold, not warm, fluid in the second step will leave greater amounts of residual film, increasing the effectiveness of the deice/anti-ice fluid.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Even a small amount of frost, ice, or snow may

choices.text: hinder lift production to a point where takeoff will be impossible.

questions.explanation: Frost does not change the aerodynamic shape of the wing. The roughness of the wing’s surface spoils the smooth flow of air, causing the airflow to slow down. This slowing of the air causes early airflow separation over the affected airfoil. This results in a loss of lift. A small amount of frost on airfoils may prevent an aircraft from becoming airborne at normal takeoff speed or hinder the production of lift to the point that takeoff will be impossible altogether. It is also possible that if the aircraft becomes airborne, it could have an insufficient margin of airspeed above stall so that moderate gusts or turning the aircraft could produce incipient or complete stalling. Answer (A) is incorrect. Test data indicate that ice, snow, or frost having a thickness and roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of a wing can reduce lift by as much as 30% and increase drag by 40%. This will decrease takeoff performance, not increase it. Answer (C) is incorrect. Extra drag caused by ice, snow, or frost having a thickness and roughness similar to medium or coarse sandpaper on the leading edge and upper surface of a wing can reduce lift by as much as 30% and increase drag by 40%. This will require an increased takeoff ground run. Even with an increased takeoff ground run, the aircraft may not take off at all.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Deicing procedures and equipment developed for large transport airplanes

choices.text: Will not be appropriate for the smaller aircraft, used under 14 CFR Part 135.
Will be appropriate for all of the smaller aircraft, used under 14 CFR Part 135.
May not be appropriate for some of the smaller aircraft, used under 14 CFR Part 135.

questions.explanation: Deicing procedures and equipment developed for large transport airplanes may not be appropriate for some of the smaller aircraft used under 14 CFR Part 135. Answer (A) is incorrect. Deicing procedures and equipment developed for large transport airplanes may not be appropriate for some, not all, of the smaller aircraft used under 14 CFR Part 135. Answer (B) is incorrect. Deicing procedures and equipment developed for large transport airplanes may be appropriate for some, not all, of the smaller aircraft used under 14 CFR Part 135.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: During an en route descent, both the ram air input and drain hole of the pitot system become completely blocked by ice. What airspeed indication can be expected?

choices.text: Indicated airspeed remains at the value prior to icing.

questions.explanation: If the ram air input and the drain hole are blocked, the pressure is trapped in the system, and the airspeed indicator will react as an altimeter. During a descent, the airspeed indication will decrease. Answer (A) is incorrect. Indicated airspeed will decrease, not increase, in a descent. Answer (B) is incorrect. Indicated airspeed will remain at the same value during level, not descending, flight.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: During a constant-rate climb in IMC above the freezing level, you notice that both the airspeed and altitude are increasing. This indicates the

choices.text: aircraft is in an unusual attitude.

questions.explanation: If the pitot tube and its drain hole are blocked, then as the aircraft climbs, the trapped air in the pitot system will be compared against decreasing air pressure in the static system. The airspeed indication will rise, but it will not be accurate. If the aircraft descends, the airspeed indication will decrease. When this happens, the airspeed indicator behaves like an altimeter. Answer (A) is incorrect. If the aircraft were in an unusual attitude, the altimeter and airspeed would not be simultaneously increasing. Answer (B) is incorrect. The gyroscopic instruments are not interconnected with the pitot and static instruments.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: What can a pilot expect if the pitot system ram air input and drain hole are blocked by ice?

choices.text: The airspeed indicator may act as an altimeter.
The airspeed indicator will show a decrease with an increase in altitude.
No airspeed indicator change will occur during climbs or descents.

questions.explanation: If the ram air and the drain hole are blocked, the pressure is trapped in the system, and the airspeed indicator will react as an altimeter: higher indicated airspeed at higher altitudes and lower indicated airspeed at lower altitudes. Answer (B) is incorrect. The airspeed indicator will show an increase, not decrease, with an increase in altitude. Answer (C) is incorrect. Differential pressure between the pitot tube and static air source changes and so does indicated airspeed.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: How will the airspeed indicator react if the ram air input to the pitot head is blocked by ice, but the drain hole and static port are not?

choices.text: Indication will rise to the top of the scale.
Indication will remain constant but will increase in a climb.

questions.explanation: If the ram air input to the pitot head is blocked by ice but the drain hole and static port remain open, the pressure in the line to the airspeed indicator will vent out through the drain hole. Thus, the airspeed indication will drop to zero. Answer (B) is incorrect. The airspeed indication will drop to zero, not rise to the top of the scale, if only the ram air input is blocked. Answer (C) is incorrect. The pressure in the airspeed line will vent out through the vent hole, and the indication will drop to zero. It will not act as an altimeter.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: If both the ram air input and drain hole of the pitot system become blocked, the indicated airspeed will

choices.text: remain constant regardless of altitude change.

questions.explanation: If both the pitot tube input and the drain hole on the pitot system are blocked, the airspeed indication will increase in a climb and decrease in a descent. Answer (B) is incorrect. During a climb, it will indicate an increase, not decrease, due to the stronger differential pressure in the blocked pitot tube relative to the static vents. Answer (C) is incorrect. Indicated airspeed will change with changes in altitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When setting the altimeter, pilots should disregard

choices.text: effects of nonstandard atmospheric temperatures and pressures.

questions.explanation: When setting the altimeter, pilots should disregard the effects of nonstandard atmospheric temperatures and pressures. The altimeter setting system provides a means that corrects for pressure variations. Since instrument flight in controlled airspace is accomplished at assigned indicated altitudes, airplane separation is maintained because all aircraft using the same altimeter setting are equally affected by nonstandard temperatures and pressures equally at various levels. Answer (B) is incorrect. Altimeters are subject to errors in the static pressure system. A pilot should set the current reported altimeter setting on the altimeter setting scale. The altimeter should read within 75 ft. of field elevation. If not, it is questionable and should be evaluated by a repair station. Answer (C) is incorrect. Altimeters are subject to instrument errors. A pilot should set the current reported altimeter setting on the altimeter setting scale. The altimeter should read within 75 ft. of field elevation. If not, it is questionable and should be evaluated by a repair station.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When the temperature is -20°C at 15,000 feet indicated, you know that

choices.text: altimeters automatically compensate for temperature variations.
the altimeter is indicating higher than true altitude.
the altimeter is indicating lower than true altitude.

questions.explanation: The ISA for 15,000 feet is -15°C. When the temperature is colder than standard, the altimeter will indicate a higher than true altitude. Answer (A) is incorrect. Altimeters do not compensate for temperature variations. Answer (C) is incorrect. When the temperature is warmer than standard, the altimeter will indicate a lower than true altitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Moving map displays

choices.text: May or may not be accurate.
Are certified to be accurate on a small scale setting.
Are very accurate and require no current chart overlays for precise navigation.

questions.explanation: The moving map display is designed to provide supplemental navigation information but is not approved as a substitute for primary navigation instruments. While the primary navigation CDI and related system components are required to meet certification standards for accuracy of information, moving map displays are not. Thus, a moving map may or may not be accurate depending on the accuracy of the information being fed to it by the navigation source. Answer (B) is incorrect. Moving map displays are not required to meet any certification standards in terms of accuracy. Also, the scale setting of the moving map has no impact on its accuracy. The accuracy of the displayed position is based on the navigation sensitivity supplied by the unit feeding positional information to the moving map. Answer (C) is incorrect. Not only is a moving map not required to meet any certification standards for accuracy, but database currency is essential for effective situational awareness. In IFR operations, database currency is a requisite of using the device.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An airspeed vertical tape display

choices.text: Is blank if the aircraft is in icing condition.
Will freeze when a stall is encountered.
Scrolls down to show an increase in airspeed.

questions.explanation: The vertical airspeed tape is configured so that lower speeds are at the bottom of the tape and higher speeds are at the top of the tape. This means that while airspeed is increasing, the airspeed tape is actually scrolling down so that higher numbers are appearing. Answer (A) is incorrect. The airspeed tape will indicate a failure if the pitot and/or static inputs are blocked by ice, but it will not automatically go blank as soon as icing conditions are encountered. Answer (B) is incorrect. The airspeed tape is constantly in motion as long as pitot-static inputs are being received.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: The message “NAV service not communicating” on a moving map display means that the

choices.text: NAV source will be reset when the message is acknowledged.
Selected NAV source is not publishing data to the display.

questions.explanation: Failure indications on the moving map can be quite subtle. The moving map will reflect a loss of position information by the removal of the aircraft symbol, compass labels, and other small differences. A message of some sort will also appear, alerting the pilot that the navigation source is not providing data to the display unit. Answer (A) is incorrect. A moving map display is not a control unit; it is only a display unit. Acknowledging a message has no effect on the system that sent the message. The only way to reset the NAV source in this case would be to troubleshoot the source itself, not the moving map display. Answer (C) is incorrect. This message does not necessarily mean that the GPS is inoperative, merely that it is not communicating with the moving map display. You could easily troubleshoot the GPS unit by reviewing the satellite status page to ensure it was operating correctly.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 998 on the inside back cover.) You see the indication in the figure on your PFD, but your standby indicator reads 120 knots and the power is set for 120-knot cruise in level flight. You decide the

choices.text: pitot tube may be plugged with ice or a bug.
standby indicator is defective because there is no red ‘X’ on the speed tape display.

questions.explanation: Because your attitude, power setting, and standby airspeed indicator represent a predictable flight situation, you should assume that the PFD airspeed indication is invalid. Neither the Air Data Computer (ADC) nor its components have failed because no red X is present on the PFD. It is most likely that a clog has occurred in the pitot line feeding the ADC, but after the split in the main line that also feeds the standby indicator. Answer (B) is incorrect. A red X would only appear over the PFD airspeed indication if the ADC or its components had failed entirely. It is possible that the pitot line feeding the ADC is blocked, thus rendering the ADC and the PFD airspeed indication inaccurate. Because the aircraft’s attitude and power setting agree with the indication on the standby indicator, it is more reliable than the PFD indication. Answer (C) is incorrect. The power setting and the standby airspeed indicator reflect normal cruise flight. By cross-checking your other cockpit instrumentation, you can quickly rule out the possibility of an incorrect flight attitude.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 999 on the inside back cover.) The MFD in the figure has lost
questions.explanation: In the lower right-hand corner of Fig. 999, the message “NAV Source Not Communicating” indicates that the moving map is not currently displaying positional information. Other clues to this are the removal of the aircraft symbol and the compass rose. Answer (A) is incorrect. Even though no traffic is shown on the moving map, no indication is provided that traffic information is not being shown due to a failure of either the traffic system or the moving map itself. Answer (C) is incorrect. The Air Data Computer (ADC) provides airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, and other flight information to the PFD. A failure of the ADC would result in red Xs on the PFD but have no bearing on the MFD.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When flying an aircraft with Electronic Flight Displays (EFDs), risk increases

choices.text: when the pilot trusts the equipment to malfunction on occasion.
if the pilot believes the EFD will compensate for lack of skill and knowledge.
if the pilot does not expect the electronics to enhance flight safety by removing pilot error.

questions.explanation: EFDs do not replace basic flight knowledge and skills. EFDs are tools for improving flight safety. Risk increases when the pilot believes the system will compensate for lack of knowledge and skill. It is important to recognize that there are limits to what the EFD systems can do. Being pilot in command requires sound aeronautical decision making which sometimes means saying “no” to a flight. Answer (A) is incorrect. It is good for a pilot to know that on occasion, equipment may malfunction. When equipment fails during flight, the pilot’s skill and knowledge of the system can overcome that equipment failure. Answer (C) is incorrect. EFDs are meant to simplify tasks the pilot has to perform and should enhance flight safety. The pilot has to vigilantly monitor the systems, or pilot error will come about.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Automation in aircraft has proven

choices.text: to be able to create larger errors.

questions.explanation: The Veillette-Decker study on automation found that while automation made the promise of reducing human mistakes, in some instances it actually created larger errors. Answer (B) is incorrect. Automation can actually foster deterioration of basic piloting skills and lead to much larger errors at times. Answer (C) is incorrect. Automation can actually lead to increased complacency.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Automation has been found to

choices.text: create much larger errors at times.
substitute for a lack of aviation experience.

questions.explanation: The Veillette-Decker study on automation found that while automation made the promise of reducing human mistakes, in some instances it actually created larger errors. Answer (B) is incorrect. Automation by itself does not improve crew situational awareness; rather, automation can actually foster deterioration of basic piloting skills and lead to much larger errors at times. Answer (C) is incorrect. Automation is not a substitute for a lack of aviation experience. In fact, it has been shown that automation can actually lead to much larger errors at times.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: Automation has been found to

choices.text: create higher workloads in terminal areas.
substitute for a lack of aviation experience.

questions.explanation: One of the surprising findings of the Veillette-Decker study was that automation could actually create a higher workload in the terminal area than would be experienced in an older aircraft with a conventional flight deck. Answer (B) is incorrect. Automation does not inherently provide crews with a heightened sense of situational awareness or the skills necessary to improve situational awareness. Answer (C) is incorrect. Automation is not a substitute for a lack of aviation experience.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: When using cockpit or flight deck automation, always

choices.text: use the information presented to make all of the flight decisions.
trust the displays, since computers do not make mistakes like humans.

questions.explanation: A good strategy for maintaining situational awareness information management should include practices that help ensure that awareness is enhanced by the use of automation, not diminished. At a minimum, ensure the presentation makes sense. Answer (A) is incorrect. Using the information presented to make all of the flight decisions could lead to an incident or accident, e.g., following the moving map’s magenta line that gives no terrain avoidance information or flying close to a restricted airspace that is depicted on a moving map to find out that you were inside that airspace with a notification from ATC with an 800 number for you to call after you land. Answer (C) is incorrect. The programs used in computers are written by humans. If the presentation does not make sense, don’t use it.

questions.subject: Aerodynamics and Airplanes
questions.question: An aircraft that is equipped with an Electronic Flight Display (EFD) can

choices.text: compensate for an airman’s lack of skill or knowledge.
offer new capabilities and simplify the basic flying task.
improve flight awareness by allowing the pilot to simply watch for alerts.

questions.explanation: EFDs offer new capabilities, such as enhanced situational awareness, and simplify basic flying tasks, such as traditional cross-country flight planning and fuel management. Answer (A) is incorrect. It is important to remember that EFDs do not replace basic flight knowledge and skills. They are a tool for improving flight safety. Risk increases when a pilot believes the EFD will compensate for a lack of skill or knowledge. It is especially important to recognize there are limits to what electronic systems in any light GA aircraft can do. Being pilot in command requires sound aeronautical decision making, which sometimes means saying no to a flight. Answer (C) is incorrect. An advanced avionics aircraft offers increased safety with enhanced situational awareness. Tools such as the moving map, topography, terrain awareness, traffic, and weather datalink displays, give the pilot unprecedented information for enhanced situational awareness, but, without a well-planned information management strategy, these tools also make it easy for an unwary pilot to slide into the complacent role of “passenger in command.”
